title: Miami Dolphins vs. Buffalo Bills: Three Reasons Why
summary: This week has not been kind to the making of content for this post.  The flow of hope for getting win from here on out is down to a trickle.  Let’s see if we can salvage any for this contest. 3 REASONS THE DOLPHINS WILL WIN THE BILLS PASS DEFENSE IS SUSCEPTIBLE The Bills pass […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MN - OCTOBER 04: Miami Dolphins wide receiver Malik Washington (6) muffs a punt during the first half of the NFL game between the Miami Dolphins and the Minnesota Vikings on October 4th, 2026, at U.S. Bank Stadium in Minneapolis, MN. (Photo by Bailey Hillesheim/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images This week has not been kind to the making of content for this post. The flow of hope for getting win from here on out is down to a trickle. Let’s see if we can salvage any for this contest. 3 REASONS THE DOLPHINS WILL WIN THE BILLS PASS DEFENSE IS SUSCEPTIBLE The Bills pass defense has been the weaker part of their defense this season. They had games against Joey Fagnano and Carson Wentz where they held them to under 200 combined yards. But they have allowed 250+ passing yards to just about everyone else. Last week, Kyle McCord made his debut against a weak Colts defense and played alright. He threw for 209 yards and got the RBs involved in the passing game. I don’t expect McCord to light it up, but he has the opportunity for some success against a middle of the pack pass defense. THE BILLS TURN THE BALL OVER Despite being one of two 8-1 teams in the league, they have a turnover differential of zero. They have 14 takeaways and 14 giveaways. QB Josh Allen is playing well, particularly as a rusher, leading the team with 11 rushing TDs. He is in the middle of the pack for passing TDs. But he has 7 INTS and 4 fumbles on the season. James Cook has 4 fumbles this season. Turnovers are the great equalizer, and Miami is getting better at generating them. The Dolphins have generated at least one turnover in each of the last 5 games. All it takes is for one errant throw or fumbled ball to swing momentum and turn the tide. POTENTIAL DIVISIONAL TRAP GAME I generally don’t think divisional games can be trap games, but the odds for that are never zero. The Bills face the 7-2 Chiefs the following week. Then go on the road to face New England, Green Bay, before facing Chicago and Denver. Part of me thinks Buffalo will look at this game as a must win – the final “gimme game” before a slate of playoff bound opponents. Another part of me thinks they can be looking ahead to the Chiefs and might slip up. The 1-8 Dolphins led by Kyle McCord will be easy to overlook. But if the defense steps up just enough, they can make this a tougher out than expected. 3 REASONS THE DOLPHINS WILL LOSE DECIMATION ACROSS THE LINE Miami lost 3 of their top interior defensive linemen in the span of a week. Sieler, Phillips, and Biggers are out for the season. The Dolphins are stuck relying on Kenneth Grant and some guys. The current IDL on the roster are Grant, Keith Cooper Jr., and Jordan Jefferson. They have some bigger edge players like Eric Watts (6’5” 277) and Rodney McGraw (6’4”, 273) that can perhaps move inside on some passing downs. They can also big the bigger edge players in run defense. Miami also signed Matthew Butler to the practice squad. Butler was with the Dolphins in 2025 and in camp this offseason before being cut. He adds some depth and scheme familiarity. But the Bills have one of the better offensive lines, ranked 3rd in pass block win rate and 1st in run block win rate. The Bills are the 3rd in rushing attempts, 2nd in rushing yards, 6th in yards per attempt, and 1st in rushing TDs. The Dolphins run defense had a solid game against Jahmyr Gibbs and the Lions, but had their worst outing against the Colts, allowing 172 yards, the most in any game this season. Some good news is that Grant and Cooper both had solid games against the Colts. But even if they play out of their minds this week, it is still a horrible matchup for the Dolphins. MIAMI’S OFFENSIVE LINE IS REGRESSING The Bills are at the top in terms of winning pass and run blocks. On the defensive side, they are less so. They are currently 29th in pass rush win rate and 23rd in run stop win rate. That said, the Dolphins’ run offense is stagnating. They haven’t rushed for more than 78 yards in any of the last 3 games. Having an injured Malik Willis contributed to that. However, after an early breakout for Ollie Gordon II, he has been limited to under 4 YPC in the last 3 games. Part of that for last week could be having a backup QB as the starter – defenses will worry more about the run. But part of that is the offensive line. The Lions and Pats were better run defenses. The Colts were not – one of the worst in the league and the Dolphins still couldn’t get going on the ground The offensive line has to take their share of that blame. Starting center Aaron Brewer missed last week in concussion protocol and did not practice Wednesday. He returned Thursday, but hasn’t cleared protocol just yet. His backup, Andrew Meyer, was bad against a good-not-great Colts front. Meyer was also a problem with the batted balls for McCord that cost Miami some big plays, including a potential TD. RG Jonah Savaiinaea looked like an improved player early on but has been moving in the opposite direction. In the passing game, the Bills aren’t high at the win rate, but they are 4th in the league in pressure percentage at 28%. They are tied with 4 other teams at 17th for sacks with 21. They only have 2 players with more than 1.5 sacks on the season. BUT… they have one of the league’s top rushers in Gregory Rousseau, who is tied for 4th with 8 sacks on the season. He leads the league in pressures with 37. He is NOT in the top 22 in pass rush win rate, which would lead me to believe he is getting pressures and sacks due to volume – only 4 other teams have as many or more pass attempts against them than the Bills. This leads back to Miami’s OL and Austin Jackson. He has been a liability against every top edge rusher he has faced; Aidan Hutchinson took his lunch money 2 weeks ago. Now he has to face Rousseau, who may not win as early and as often as Hutchinson but still gets to the QB. If the Dolphins can’t keep the Bills defense honest by running the ball and/or get too far behind, the Bills pass rush is very likely to heat up McCord. MIAMI DOESN’T WIN IN BUFFALO Do you remember the last time Miami won in Buffalo? I certainly do. It was the 2016 season where the Dolphins snuck out an overtime win thanks to Jay Ajayi rushing for 206 yards on 32 carries and some heroic kicks made by Andrew Franks. Outside of that game, the Dolphins haven’t had much success on the road against Buffalo. Since 2000, the Dolphins have played in Buffalo 27 times including the playoffs and have gotten 7 wins. They haven’t beaten Josh Allen in Buffalo, but this isn’t just about the Allen-led Bills. From 2000 until 2019, when Allen took over as the full-time starter, the Bills had 3 winning seasons and they were 9-7 seasons. They had three 8-8 seasons. Their record was 127-177 and the average season was 6.7 wins and 9.3 losses. Allen has started 9 games against the Dolphins in Buffalo, so that’s still 7 wins in the other 18 attempts. When they DID win, the average record for Buffalo was 6-10. The average margin of victory in those games was 10.7, and it’s been 7 or less in the last 3 times. So even when Buffalo was mid, the Dolphins still couldn’t win there. They absolutely haven’t won there any time Buffalo has finished with a winning record. The last time the Dolphins won in Buffalo in the same season Buffalo finished with a winning record was 1996. This week, the Dolphins take a talent deficient team that is now weaker due to injuries and starting a backup QB in his second ever NFL game on the road to a place they don’t win at, even when the opponent is bad. Now… the last 2 times Miami has marched into Buffalo with a backup QB starting the game, they have a record of 1-1. They got their last win with Matt Moore starting for Ryan Tannehill. Skylar Thompson went into Buffalo in the playoffs and fell just short, losing 34-31. If there is ANY hope in this regard, it’s that recent history shows Miami backups making the game a tougher…

That came with one full practice under his belt, no Jordan Addison, no T.J. Hockenson, and no Jauan Jennings. This week, Hockenson and Jennings will be back. . .and I have a feeling that this is the week where Jennings finally makes his way out of the Witness Protection Program. . .and Cousins might even know the names of everyone that he’s in the huddle with. On top of that, the Niners have not recorded a quarterback sack in a full calendar month. Yes, Cousins threw three interceptions against this same Niners’ defense just a couple of weeks ago. . .I don’t see that happening again this week. Take the over. Justin Jefferson Receiving Yards : Over 84.5 (-114) Yes, I know I also took the over on Jefferson’s receiving yards last week, and he came up just short. The Cousins-to-Jefferson connection is going to be big this week. Jefferson’s last 100-yard game came in the regular season finale last year when the Vikings were force-feeding him the ball to get him over the 1,000-yard mark for the season. His last 100-yard game before that? Week 5 of last year, when the Vikings faced the Cleveland Browns in London. We’re going to see Jefferson go over the century mark in this one, I think. Take the over on this one, too. Parlay : Vikings +3.5 and under 46.5 (+241) It worked last week, so why not go for it again this week? This is the fourth week in a row that the Vikings go into the game as an underdog, and with Kirk Cousins in the fold. . .well, this team can, honestly, beat any team in the NFL if they can sustain a few drives here and there. As far as the over/under? Well, the Vikings have still only had one game go “over” all season, and that was the Week 1 game against the Packers. Anyone who bets the “over” on a Vikings game at this point deserves to lose their money, and I don’t want you to be that person, so we’ll just stick with the over until someone gives us reason not to. Those are the prop bets we’re looking at for this week’s game, ladies and gentlemen. Are there any that you have your eyes on?

Historically, 95% of players designated probable are active and played on game day. Questionable = the league defines a Questionable injury designation as being ‘uncertain’ of whether the player will play or not. This replaces the former definition of having a 50% chance of playing. title: Minnesota Doesn’t Need Superhero Kirk. It Needs Consistent Kirk.
summary: The Vikings can beat the 49ers—but which Kirk Cousins will show up? That question drives this episode of The Real Forno Show, as Tyler Forness and producer Dave Stefano break down Minnesota’s offensive path to victory in Mexico City. On this Vikings 1st & SKOL production, the discussion moves beyond revenge-game narratives to the matchups […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - NOVEMBER 15: Kirk Cousins #8 of the Minnesota Vikings looks on against the Green Bay Packers during the fourth quarter at Lambeau Field on November 15, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Vikings can beat the 49ers—but which Kirk Cousins will show up? That question drives this episode of The Real Forno Show , as Tyler Forness and producer Dave Stefano break down Minnesota’s offensive path to victory in Mexico City. On this Vikings 1st & SKOL production, the discussion moves beyond revenge-game narratives to the matchups that could decide the game: pass protection, attacking single-high coverage, and keeping Fred Warner from wrecking the passing attack. “There is a pathway for the Minnesota Vikings offense to beat the San Francisco 49ers,” Forness declares. However, that pathway requires something more dependable than occasional quarterback brilliance. Cousins doesn’t need to carry the Vikings by himself. Instead, Forness argues that Minnesota needs repeatable execution from a quarterback whose best moments can rival anyone’s. “He can just be a point guard,” Forness explains. “He can just be a guy who distributes the football to the weapons.” That starts with Christian Darrisaw and Brian O’Neill protecting against a San Francisco pass rush that the hosts describe as inconsistent. From there, Minnesota can attack Cover 1 and Cover 3 with intermediate in-breaking routes, dagger concepts, and seams featuring Justin Jefferson, T.J. Hockenson, and Jauan Jennings. Warner remains the major complication: his coverage range can erase those opportunities unless Kevin O’Connell uses underneath routes to draw him forward. Meanwhile, Jennings and Jordan Mason offer compelling former-team storylines—and practical ways to move the ball. Key takeaways from the episode: Consistency matters more than perfection. Forness separates Cousins’ talent from his game-to-game execution. Stefano adds that maturity could help the veteran remain “relatively calm and collected.” Protection unlocks the passing game. Keeping Nick Bosa and the 49ers’ defensive front away from Cousins would give Minnesota more chances to exploit coverage downfield. Make Warner defend forward and backward. Shallow concepts can occupy the linebacker, creating opportunities behind him rather than allowing him to drift into throwing lanes. Jennings can expand the quick game. Forness highlights screens, stick routes, short in-breakers, and selective slants as ways to capitalize on the receiver’s physicality. Mason could influence the game script. A productive rushing attack would challenge his former team while reducing the number of demanding routes Minnesota’s receivers run at altitude. Mexico City preparation matters. The hosts debate Minnesota’s altitude-chamber training, hydration, recovery, and the benefit of sleeping at home before traveling. The prediction: Minnesota wins 24–17. Still, Forness acknowledges San Francisco’s quality and makes clear that a 49ers victory would not surprise him. Listen: View Link Or on your favorite podcast aggregator. Watch: For Vikings fans seeking more than a box-score argument, this episode connects quarterback expectations with the route concepts, blocking assignments, and personnel decisions that could shape the matchup. As Forness puts it, “It just has to be good. That’s all we’re asking, just be good.” Stefano supplies the essential addition: “Be good and score some points.” Watch or listen to The Real Forno Show with Tyler Forness and Dave Stefano, a Minnesota Vikings podcast from Vikings 1st & SKOL, for the full discussion and debate. Fan with Us!!! Tyler Forness @TheRealForno of Vikings 1st & SKOL @Vikings1stSKOL and A to Z Sports @AtoZSportsNFL , with Dave Stefano @Luft_Krigare producing this Vikings 1st & SKOL production, the @RealFornoShow found at the @BleavNetwork . So here’s the question, Vikings fans: Which will matter most against San Francisco: Cousins’ consistency, Jennings’ physicality, or Mason powering the running game?

title: Daniel Jones has been released by the Colts. Should the Patriots go after him?
summary: You heard about a Friday news dump, but have you heard about a Friday QB dump? That’s precisely what the Indianapolis Colts did when they released their starting quarterback, Daniel Jones, earlier today. Jones, 29, was in his second season with the franchise and just eight months removed from signing a two-year, $88 million contract […]
full_text: You heard about a Friday news dump, but have you heard about a Friday QB dump? That’s precisely what the Indianapolis Colts did when they released their starting quarterback , Daniel Jones, earlier today. Jones, 29, was in his second season with the franchise and just eight months removed from signing a two-year, $88 million contract extension. However, he and the Colts as a whole have struggled mightily this year, leading to some sweeping changes within the organization. First, they fired the GM who signed him to that deal, Chris Ballard, and now they let go of Jones himself. His release comes with the Colts at 3-8 and Jones having completed 205 of 351 pass attempts (58.4%) for 1,974 yards with seven touchdowns and 13 interceptions. A year removed from tearing his Achilles tendon, he is ranked 30th among 31 qualifying quarterbacks in EPA per play this season (-0.139) and 31st in both net yards per attempt (4.8) and completion percentage above expectation (-6.1). Long story short, he has been dreadful. And yet, the New England Patriots might just keep a close eye on him. The Patriots, after all, saw their own starting QB, Drake Maye, suffer a fractured fibula during last Sunday’s loss versus the Detroit Lions. While it remains to be seen how long he will be out, Maye missing most if not all of his team’s seven final regular season games this year would not come as a surprise. The question now becomes whether or not the Patriots should pursue Jones as a replacement. Let’s make the argument in favor of and against such a move. Why the Patriots should sign Daniel Jones Before making this argument, it needs to be prefaced with this: everything in this section only applies to Jones going through the waiver wire unclaimed and making it to the open market. According to Jason Fitzgerald of Over the Cap, a team would need $6.35 million in salary cap space to claim Jones — financial flexibility the Patriots do not have at the moment. If he passes waivers, he could be signed to a deal worth as little as $505,554. With that out of the way, let’s take a look at why brining Jones in would make sense for the Patriots. It all starts with one question: would he be an upgrade over Tommy DeVito for however long Drake Maye will be sidelined? His play this season so far suggests that that might not be the case. However, a change in environment might help Jones regain some of the confidence he had in his first year with the Colts, when he played some of the best football of his career and finished the season sixth in the league in EPA per play (0.201). If the Patriots can get a fraction of that, they should be happy with Jones as a better alternative than DeVito. In addition, Jones also has some familiarity with the Patriots scheme. While he never played directly under offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels, he did spend the better part of three seasons under former New England assistant Brian Daboll. The offense Daboll ran with the Giants has similarities to McDaniels’ in terms of terminology, quarterback responsibility and play designs, meaning that the lead-up time for Jones to get ready would be comparatively small. Inserting Jones would likely also not come with significant philosophical changes. In essence, after all, he is a similar player type as Maye is: somebody capable of making plays with his arm as well as his legs, as evidenced by his career rushing average of 6.1 yards per carry. While his highs have not been close to Maye’s, he has shown that he can be an adequate NFL starting quarterback and somebody able to elevate the talent around him. That obviously was not the case in Indianapolis this season, but if a change of scenery and move to a better-run team can get him close to that, it would be precisely what the Patriots need right now if there are any doubts about DeVito. And even if not, what do the Patriots have to lose? They are 5-5 and fighting for their playoff lives, and signing Jones would not automatically disqualify them from starting DeVito. At the very least, he would provide veteran depth better suited to challenge the post-Maye hierarchy than sixth-round rookie Behren Morton. Why the Patriots shouldn’t sign Daniel Jones On Friday, Jones became the first quarterback in the NFL in more than three decades to get released less than 24 hours after starting a game. That plus the fact the Colts are willing to cut their losses despite the financial investment they made in him just this offseason should tell you all you need to know. It’s been bad this year. Very, very bad. While there might be a snowballing effect to Jones’ struggles and a fresh start could indeed help him regain the form he previously showed, there is no denying he has played some of the worst football in the NFL this year. The numbers mentioned above are an illustration of that. Some of it had to do with the surroundings and a Colts team that a) lacking quality across the board, and b) is in a free fall since October. In addition, his injury situation also seems to have played a part in it: 12 months after his torn Achilles, he still does not look like he is close to 100% and fails to consistently to step into throws, maneuver the pocket and pick up yards on the ground, averaging just 3.8 yards per carry. On top of it, Jones has been a streaky player throughout his career. While there have been stretches of play where he lived up to his former first-round status, the lows have been underwhelming, including this season. Given all of that, expecting a quick turnaround in New England would be naive, particularly considering that the Patriots are missing several offensive pieces because of injury. But even if they didn’t, Jones would not have any familiarity with them: despite some experience in a McDaniels-style system, he would have to build chemistry with his receiving corps, offensive line and coaching staff on the fly. Tommy DeVito, meanwhile, has a two-year head start in that regard. Speaking of DeVito, he was signed to a contract extension in the offseason to serve as QB2 and has, by all accounts, been a model citizen deserving of his shot. Obviously, the job should go to the best option regardless of contract situation. That said, all things considered — including what a change might mean for the locker room — DeVito still has a strong case to be just that. Verdict Even though they are still in a competitive position on paper, the Patriots are fighting for their playoff lives with Drake Maye sidelined for the foreseeable future. Their margin for error, meanwhile, is, to quote safety Kevin Byard, “basically at zero.” Would adding Jones increase it and allow New England to play winning football during Maye’s absence? Ideally, that is not a question they would have to ask; Tommy DeVito stepping in and leading the offense at an adequate level would be the best-case scenario. Of course, as the Lions game showed, there is a realistic chance the lights are too bright for him. The problem is, they also might be for Jones. So far this season, after all, he has not been good and not been able to hold up to the pressure of being the guy at quarterback in Indianapolis. He wouldn’t quite be that in New England, sure, but the eyes of one of the NFL’s biggest markets would still be on him. Would that prevent the Patriots from signing him? Probably not. Still, it is one of the factors to consider alongside the arguments outlined above. And putting all of those together, it is clear the decision whether or not to sign Jones as a potential stand-in for Maye is quite nuanced. At the end of the day, Mike Vrabel, Eliot Wolf and Ryan Cowden — the latter of whom spent time with Jones in New York — will have to see their way through it. And once they do, they very well might find that the potential disruption caused by adding Jones might not be worth the theoretical gains. What do you think about Daniel Jones? Should the Patriots pursue him, or steer clear of him? Please head down to the comment…

title: A.J. Brown injury update: Patriots WR to miss multiple weeks
summary: The hits keep on coming for the New England Patriots and their marquee offseason trade acquisition. Wide receiver A.J. Brown, who joined the team in a trade with the Philadelphia Eagles in April, is expected to be sidelined “multiple weeks” due to the hamstring injury he suffered last Sunday against the Detroit Lions. Mike Reiss […]
full_text: The hits keep on coming for the New England Patriots and their marquee offseason trade acquisition. Wide receiver A.J. Brown, who joined the team in a trade with the Philadelphia Eagles in April, is expected to be sidelined “multiple weeks” due to the hamstring injury he suffered last Sunday against the Detroit Lions. Mike Reiss and Adam Schefter of ESPN were first to report the severity of the ailment. Brown will now have missed time due to injury on three different occasions this season. The 29-year-old previously suffered a high ankle sprain in the third quarter of New England’s season opener against the Seattle Seahawks, and was placed on injured reserve shortly thereafter. After sitting out four games, he made his return in Week 6 but only appeared in two games before missing time with a knee issue. He sat out the next two contests before making his comeback against the Lions. After just his second of the day, a 21-yarder in the third quarter, he exited with the aforementioned hamstring issue. Brown did not return to the contest and was ruled out a short time later, joining quarterback Drake Maye on a long list of Patriots who got hurt in the eventual 35-10 defeat. How much time Brown will ultimately miss remains to be seen. However, for the time being, he will not be able to add to his current stat-line: playing 160 total snaps over four games this season, he has caught 11 passes for 128 yards. The Patriots traded a 2028 first-round draft pick and a 2027 fourth-rounder to the Eagles to bring Brown aboard during the offseason.
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: Drake Maye injury: Everything we know about the Patriots QB’s status
summary: Their Week 10 game against the Detroit Lions was the worst-case scenario for the New England Patriots. Not only were they blown out with a final score of 35-10 to drop to 5-5 on the season, they also lost their starting quarterback to an injury: Drake Maye exited the game in the first quarter due […]
full_text: Their Week 10 game against the Detroit Lions was the worst-case scenario for the New England Patriots. Not only were they blown out with a final score of 35-10 to drop to 5-5 on the season, they also lost their starting quarterback to an injury: Drake Maye exited the game in the first quarter due to what was later announced as an ankle injury. Shortly after the game, information was scarce but the first bits and pieces have started to come in. Based on everything we know, here is what we can say about Maye and his injury situation. What happened? The Patriots started Sunday’s game against the Lions with the ball, and actually moved down the field relatively well; it took them only eight plays to get from their own 25-yard line to the Detroit 3. Once there, however, things started to fall apart. Two penalties bookending an incomplete pass set up a 3rd-and-goal from the 13-yard line, and that play turned into a disaster for the Patriots. Aidan Hutchinson easily got around left tackle Christian Elliss, and dragged Maye down from behind and he was climbing an increasingly collapsing pocket. Along the way, the two-time Pro Bowl edge came down on Maye’s right ankle. He did get up under his own power, but Maye showed a noticeable limp while making his way toward the sideline. Once there, he received attention from the team’s medical staff and afterwards headed into the blue medical tent. When he emerged, still clearly hobbled, backup quarterback Tommy DeVito was already getting ready to enter the game. Maye slowly walked back to the locker room shortly thereafter, and initially labeled questionable to return by the team. Midway through the second quarter, he was downgraded to out. What do we know about the injury? Neither head coach Mike Vrabel nor any of his teammates were able to provide an update on Maye’s status during their post-game media availability. “Obviously, he wasn’t able to finish the game, so we’ll have to get some more tests run and we’ll see when we come back what it ends up being and the severity of whatever injury he has,” Vrabel said at the podium. “I know that it was a low leg injury. I don’t know the exact details of it but I know he couldn’t go back in. … He couldn’t function. Couldn’t play. Couldn’t run. Couldn’t do whatever he needed to do to play quarterback, to protect himself, to execute, or function at that level.” Left tackle Will Campbell, who briefly occupied the blue medical tent before Maye went in, gave some more information in the postgame locker room. “I talked to him,” Campbell told MassLive’s Mark Daniels. “He’s in good spirits and just waiting to hear more information about what it is, and just told him I love him and praying for him and he’s going to be fine. He’s a fighter. Whatever comes his way, he’s going to attack it full head of steam and come back better.” The Patriots will fly back to the United States on Sunday, with some follow-up testing expected to take place after the team’s arrival on Monday. [UPDATE 11/16/2026] Initial reports suggest that Maye suffered a “significant lower leg injury” that might keep him out for the remainder of the season. For the Patriots, this is very much the worst-case scenario. [UPDATE 11/16/2026] The Patriots are concerned that Maye suffered a fractured ankle against the Lions. [UPDATE 11/16/2026] Drake Maye did not travel back to the United States with the rest of the Patriots, per head coach Mike Vrabel. “He’ll be traveling back here shortly. Just wanted to make sure that everything was good for him to travel back and safely. The things that go around injuries and just wanted to make sure everything was in line for him to travel, and it seems like he is. He’ll be returning here, I think, shortly.” [UPDATE 11/16/2026] If indeed diagnosed as a fractured ankle, Drake Maye would “almost certainly” be out for the rest of the season, according to a report by Ian Rapoport. [UPDATE 11/17/2026] Appearing on local radio, Patriots safety Kevin Byard said that Maye was “probably out for the season.” [UPDATE 11/19/2026] Speaking to Scott Zolak in a 1-on-1 interview, Mike Vrabel referenced Maye’s injury being a “short term” issue : “I think he’s going to be unavailable here for the short time, and we’ll see how that goes down the road.” [UPDATE 11/20/2026] According to a report by ESPN, Maye suffered a fractured fibula without any ligament damage against the Lions. While no surgery will be necessary, the injury will sideline him deep into the season if not for the remainder of the year. What does it mean for the Patriots? “Any time your starting quarterback goes out and is not able to return, there are questions,” safety Kevin Byard told the media after the game. The questions mentioned by Byard are manifold in the direct aftermath of both the injury and the contest as a whole. Information about severity or a potential recovery timeline is limited, which in turn also limits the avenues the Patriots might have to explore in the immediate or long-term future. What we do know is that for however long Maye is sidelined, Tommy DeVito will be the top quarterback on the depth chart with third-stringer Behren Morton backing him up. DeVito completed 12 of 24 pass attempts for 81 yards with one touchdown and interception each after entering the Lions game midway through the first period. DeVito described his and the offense’s performance after he took over for Maye as “not good enough.” The next chance to improve upon it will come after the Patriots’ upcoming bye, with a Sunday Night game versus the Los Angeles Chargers in Week 12. New England will not start its on-field preparation for that game until a few days beforehand; the team will return to its usual in-game schedule following the bye. [UPDATE 11/16/2026] If the injury is indeed as significant as believed, here is a rundown of how it would impact the Patriots moving forward.
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: Drake Maye injury update: Patriots QB’s diagnosis revealed
summary: Five days after he departed the New England Patriots’ game against the Detroit Lions with an injury, additional details about quarterback Drake Maye’s status have emerged. According to a report by Mike Reiss and Adam Schefter of ESPN, the 24-year-old suffered a fractured fibula without any additional ligament damage. The injury won’t require surgery but […]
full_text: Five days after he departed the New England Patriots’ game against the Detroit Lions with an injury, additional details about quarterback Drake Maye’s status have emerged. According to a report by Mike Reiss and Adam Schefter of ESPN, the 24-year-old suffered a fractured fibula without any additional ligament damage. The injury won’t require surgery but is nonetheless expected to keep Maye on the sidelines “deep into the regular season,” if he is able to return at all. Maye exited the Patriots’ game against the Lions after the opening drive. He was sacked on a third down by edge rusher Aidan Hutchinson, who subsequently tore his ACL while celebrating the takedown. Maye hobbled to the sidelines where he received additional treatment before exiting for the locker room. He was ruled out with an ankle injury shortly thereafter. Due to the injury, Maye was unable to join his teammates on the flight back from Munich. The third-year QB eventually flew back to the United States after undergoing additional preparations. “I wouldn’t imagine him being available when we come out of the bye,” head coach Mike Vrabel said earlier this week . With Maye sidelined, the Patriots turned to Tommy DeVito at quarterback. DeVito completed 12 of 24 passes for 81 yards with a touchdown and an interception as New England ended up losing 35-10 to drop to 5-5 on the year. The Patriots are currently on their bye and will visit the Los Angeles Chargers in Week 12.
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: Patriots 2026 rookie class: Performance review at Pats’ bye
summary: There are multiple reasons why the New England Patriots’ 2026 season so far has been one of ups and downs. Be it injuries, individual mistakes, coaching or a more challenging schedule, the team of head coach Mike Vrabel has had a tougher time playing winning football than it did a year ago. One other factor […]
full_text: There are multiple reasons why the New England Patriots’ 2026 season so far has been one of ups and downs. Be it injuries, individual mistakes, coaching or a more challenging schedule, the team of head coach Mike Vrabel has had a tougher time playing winning football than it did a year ago. One other factor contributing to this is the impact of the rookie class. Whereas last year’s group produced three instant starters as well as other valuable contributors, the latest batch of first-year players has not changed the team on quite the same level. Even though this means that questions do remain about the group as a whole, there have been some encouraging stretches of play as well as glimpses into a bright football. So, with no football being played at One Patriot Place this week, let’s take a look at the that rookie class to see where its members stand 10 weeks into their professional careers. Draft picks OT Caleb Lomu: The Patriots traded up in the first round of the draft to select Lomu as a future starter along their offensive line. However, with Will Campbell and Morgan Moses both entrenched into the top spots at left and right tackle, respectively, the Utah product has had to start his career primarily as a backup. He has seen his most consistent action as an eligible extra blocker but did get opportunities to replace both Campbell and Moses either late in blowouts or as an injury stand-in. In total, he has played 163 snaps between left and right tackle and generally looked good. The plan therefore seemingly remains in place: he is expected to take over as New England’s right tackle as soon as this coming offseason. | 10 games (2 starts), 31.4% offensive snaps, 14.7% special teams snaps ED Gabe Jacas: “Patience” was the theme of the offseason for New England’s second-round draft pick, who, like Caleb Lomu, was also acquired following a trade up the board. Injury recovery and contract negotiations dragged on into training camp, and when he finally took the field, Jacas did not look ready to compete. However, something started to click after the end of training camp and the start of the regular season. Since then, he has played with his hair on fire and looked like one of the best rookie edges — and one of the best defenders, period — in the class. In 10 games so far, he registered 28 quarterback pressures, including 3.5 sacks, and an interception, and leads all first-year players at his position with 14 run stops. The future is looking bright. | 10 games (0 starts), 55.5% defensive snaps, 32.0% special teams snaps TE Eli Raridon: New England had been looking for a suitable second all-around tight end for years, and it finally seems to have found one. title: College Players to Watch: Week 11
summary: The Saints are coming into a matchup on Sunday where the defense will face one of its toughest opponents. The Bears will come in looking to expose some of the biggest holes on the team. Here are some college players to watch who can help fill those holes. Interior defensive tackle is the biggest need […]
full_text: KNOXVILLE, TENNESSEE - SEPTEMBER 26: Xavier Gilliam #2 of the Tennessee Volunteers pressures Arch Manning #16 of the Texas Longhorns during a game between the Tennessee Volunteers and the Texas Longhorns at Neyland Stadium on September 26, 2026 in Knoxville, Tennessee. (Photo by Roger Wimmer/ISI Photos/ISI Photos via Getty Images) | ISI Photos via Getty Images The Saints are coming into a matchup on Sunday where the defense will face one of its toughest opponents. The Bears will come in looking to expose some of the biggest holes on the team. Here are some college players to watch who can help fill those holes. Interior defensive tackle is the biggest need for this team. At 2:30 PM on ABC, LSU will be taking on one of the best in Xavier Gilliam. So far this season, Gilliam has 6 sacks and 33 pressures from the interior, along with 11.5 TFLs. That’s something the Saints could use right now. We have spoken about Will Echoles several times, and Ole Miss will be playing against Wofford at 11 AM on SECN+, but there is another DT who needs to receive more attention, and that’s David Stone. Stone is a force in the middle for the Oklahoma Sooners, and they will be playing Texas A&M at 2:45 PM on ESPN2. So far this season, Stone has 36 tackles and 3 sacks. Of course, a true lockdown corner would be a treat for the Saints, but they currently hold the 11th position in the draft. If the season keeps going the way it is, they may find themselves in a more favorable spot to draft the No. 1 overall cornerback in the draft, and that’s Notre Dame’s Leonard Moore. Moore will be playing against SMU at 6:30 PM on NBC. Through 8 games, Moore has 19 tackles. He has an opponent completion percentage of 42% and has allowed only 112 receiving yards the entire season. There’s also Ashton Hampton. Hampton is considered one of the best corners in this draft as well, and he and the Clemson Tigers will be playing Duke on Friday at 6:30 PM on ESPN. So far this season, Hampton has 2 interceptions and 45 tackles. Both corners have great size, speed, and ball skills. Finally, the Saints have to take a look at adding a safety if there isn’t a cornerback or defensive tackle available. There will be a good group to select from. Brauntae Johnson plays with Leonard Moore at Notre Dame. Johnson is a 6’2″ safety who can cover in the slot as well as play deep. Another safety to watch out for is Jelani McDonald at Texas. McDonald and the Longhorns will be playing against Arkansas at 2:30 PM on ESPN. McDonald just had one of the best games a safety could have, recording 3 INTs against LSU in Death Valley, giving him 4 on the year. The 6’2″, 201-pound safety possesses excellent size and range to play in a secondary alongside Jonas Sanker. Who are some other players you will have your eyes on this weekend? Share your thoughts in the comments.

title: Saints vs. Bears: Key Matchups
summary: The New Orleans Saints are walking into Chicago as double-digit underdogs against the Bears. The Saints have dropped two of their last three, and their season has quickly been derailed. Now in desperate need of a win, New Orleans will face their former head coach and current Bears defensive coordinator, Dennis Allen, in a game […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LA - NOVEMBER 15: Travis Etienne Jr. #3 of the New Orleans Saints warms up before a game against the Carolina Panthers at Caesars Superdome on November 15, 2026, in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Derick Hingle/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New Orleans Saints are walking into Chicago as double-digit underdogs against the Bears. The Saints have dropped two of their last three, and their season has quickly been derailed. Now in desperate need of a win, New Orleans will face their former head coach and current Bears defensive coordinator, Dennis Allen, in a game they were completely outmatched in just a year ago. If the Saints want to steal a win, it will be by taking advantage of these key matchups. QB Tyler Shough vs. Bears pass rush Saints fans will be the first ones to tell you about Allen’s capabilities as a defensive playcaller. The former Saints head coach was known for his ability to call up exotic looks at the line of scrimmage, something that has become even more relevant this season with the massive success of Brian Flores and the Minnesota Vikings defense. Tyler Shough has been a bright spot for the Saints this season, but is coming off one of the more disappointing games of his career. Even worse for Shough and the Saints, this was against a lackluster Carolina Panthers defense. Now New Orleans will be facing a team that is top-10 in sacks and just made a massive trade for one of the best defensive linemen of the decade, Jeffrey Simmons. The Saints have worked on getting the ball out faster, and it’s improved over the weeks. But pass protection remains a major concern, and with a switch at center, right guard, and right tackle, the Saints could be in for a long day. Saints running backs vs. the Bears’ run defense I don’t think I even have to elaborate here. The Saints are a bottom-five rushing offense in the league, and are coming off a game where running backs averaged 1.5 yards per carry against one of the league’s worst run defenses in the league. Now New Orleans will be facing a team that is top-five against the run. Getting the run started has been a problem all season, and really, it’s more of a Kellen Moore issue than it is a running backs issue. But if the Saints are going to have any chance at keeping up with Chicago’s high-powered offense, it will be by controlling the game on the ground. Saints pass rush vs. QB Caleb Williams The Saints have two of the most dangerous pass rushers this season, with Carl Granderson logging 8.5 sacks and Chase Young getting 8 of his own. Fortunately for the Saints, they’ll be facing a quarterback who holds on to the ball the longest in the NFL. Unfortunately for New Orleans, Caleb Williams’ time from getting the ball and releasing it hasn’t translated into sacks. Over the last two games, Williams has been sacked just twice and has become a playmaker in the face of the pass rush. The former first overall pick’s stats haven’t looked great this season, throwing just 8 touchdowns to 5 interceptions, but he has grown into a leader and can command an offense with the best of them. If the Saints want a chance at winning this game, they’ll likely have to take down the star quarterback three or more times and create impossible goal-to-go situations.

title: Interview with the Enemy: Chicago Bears
summary: This week, the New Orleans Saints will head to Solider Field to face the Chicago Bears in Week 11 of the 2026 regular season. To break it down, Bill Zimmerman of Windy City Gridiron joins us to preview this weekend’s matchup. NJ: How legitimate are the Bears’ Super Bowl aspirations at this point in the […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - OCTOBER 19: D'Andre Swift #4 of the Chicago Bears carries the ball against the New Orleans Saints during the second half of the game at Soldier Field on October 19, 2025 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Geoff Stellfox/Getty Images) | Getty Images This week, the New Orleans Saints will head to Solider Field to face the Chicago Bears in Week 11 of the 2026 regular season. To break it down, Bill Zimmerman of Windy City Gridiron joins us to preview this weekend’s matchup. NJ: How legitimate are the Bears’ Super Bowl aspirations at this point in the season? Does it feel like this could finally be the year Chicago gets it done? BZ: The Jeffery Simmons trade changed everything as far as I’m concerned. The Bears defense was the reason they weren’t a true Super Bowl contender. Dennis Allen was largely doing it with smoke and mirrors. Yes, he had really effective blitz packages on 3 rd down, but that wasn’t sustainable in the playoffs against great teams. The offense was never a question; the defense was. With Simmons, he’s a multiplier. In just two games, we’ve seen the play improve of every defensive lineman and linebacker around him. If their front 7 can play like this, it will help a banged-up secondary that is the weakest part of the team. No one can guarantee a Super Bowl, but I do think the Bears are on the short list of true Super Bowl contenders this year (and that’s very foreign to write). NJ: Who are some notable names who will be sidelined for the Bears on Sunday against the Saints? Is there a particular area in which New Orleans could exploit? BZ: The Bears are the healthiest they’ve been in a while heading into this game. They have RB Kyle Monangai returning, which will be a huge boost for their running game, and rookie CB Malik Muhammad may not be the biggest name, but he is a key starter in their secondary. TE Cole Kmet is out for the year, and S Coby Bryant has been out since training camp. The only other notable starter who will be out is CB Kyler Gordon, who injured his shoulder against Tampa; he did finish the game, but he is now listed as out for this one. The key to stopping the Bears is to attack their cornerbacks. It’s the weakest part of the roster, but you have to make sure you are getting the ball out quickly before Jeffery Simmons collapses the pocket. NJ: How much of an impact has Dennis Allen had on turning around the Bears’ defense throughout his tenure? Have there been any decisions or coaching tendencies that have rubbed fans the wrong way? BZ: I think Dennis Allen is very popular among Bears fans, and I think he was the perfect DC hire with Ben Johnson. I think Dennis Allen is at a point where he almost certainly isn’t going to get another head coaching job. That means he should be able to pair with Johnson and be the top coaches on this coaching staff for years to come. If things go well, they’ll have an Andy Reid/Steve Spagnuolo type partnership. I think, before the Simmons trade, people had been frustrated with how Dennis Allen wanted to build his defensive line, but other than that, I think Bears fans are very happy with how he calls a game, and I think most of us understand that he got a lot more success out of his defense than the level of talent that was on the field. The best thing he’s done in Chicago is create a phenomenal third down defense. The Bears have been quite strong on third downs and it’s forcing teams to get big chunk plays on the early downs or end up punting the ball back to the Bears. NJ: Who is one Bears player you think Saints fans should keep an eye on Sunday—someone who may not receive much national attention but could have a strong performance? BZ: Offensively, I don’t think there are many names to give because Caleb Williams, Luther Burden, Colston Loveland, and Rome Odunze are their main weapons, and I think football fans are pretty familiar with all of them. I do think Kyle Monangai is going to be a big part of the offensive game plan and split carries with D’Andre Swift so Monangai is one returning from injury that I think can have a strong game. Defensively, I mentioned Muhammad, but I’ll give you Austin Booker. He was a 5th-round pick in 2024 out of Missouri, and he’s been coming into his own this year as an improved run defender and a solid pass rusher. You should hear Booker’s name at least once on Sunday, either making a TFL or a sack. NJ: According to FanDuel Sportsbook , the Bears (-720) are currently 11.5-point favorites over the Saints (+520) in Sunday’s matchup; what is your final score prediction and how do you see the game playing out? BZ: It’s really hard to imagine that the Bears don’t win this one. Ben Johnson is great on extra rest, and the Bears are healthy, and I don’t think it’s an insult to say the Bears are simply a better team than the Saints and are playing them at home. I think the question isn’t who will win or whether the Bears cover the big spread? I think the offense is going to have success regardless. I think it comes down to if you think the Saints can get points on the Bears’ defense. If you do, then there’s no reason to think this one couldn’t be like 31 to 21 or so, and the Saints cover. Personally, I do think the Saints will struggle on offense against the Bears, and I think the Bears will win this one comfortably by 2 or 3 scores. I’ll call it 31 to 13. Thank you again to Bill Zimmerman for joining us to preview this week’s matchup! You can check out the rest of his work here .

title: Saints Draft Position: NFL Week 11
summary: Last season, even when the New Orleans Saints were consistently losing, their draft pick was not moving much because of how bad other teams were. This season is similar, and as of writing this, 12 teams only have 3 wins. It creates a situation where the Saints will barely move if they lose because everyone […]
full_text: IOWA CITY, IA - NOVEMBER 22: Offensive lineman Kade Pieper #58 of the Iowa Hawkeyes before the match-up against the Michigan State Spartans at Kinnick Stadium on November 22, 2025 in Iowa City, Iowa. (Photo by Matthew Holst/Getty Images) | Getty Images Last season, even when the New Orleans Saints were consistently losing, their draft pick was not moving much because of how bad other teams were. This season is similar, and as of writing this, 12 teams only have 3 wins. It creates a situation where the Saints will barely move if they lose because everyone else is also losing. So, looking at their current draft position, the Saints are set to select at pick 11 overall. For this edition, I wanted to do a trade back to the mid-20s and look at the prospects there. OL Kade Pieper First, let’s start with the offensive line. Sadly, Jeremiah Wright has not secured the Saints RG spot, and Cesar Ruiz could be on his way out. Erik McCoy’s time in New Orleans may also be coming to an end soon, which would leave the Saints having to fill both center and right guard. In the draft, Iowa offensive lineman Kade Pieper would make perfect sense as an option. He was a star at RG for Iowa, becoming a first-team All-American. This season, he was moved to center and is playing well there. He will allow the Saints some flexibility, playing RG his rookie year and potentially moving to center if McCoy leaves in 2028. LB Kyngstonn Viliamu-Asa Next is on defense. LB is an underrated need for the Saints with how well Kaden Elliss has played, but they need to find someone to put next to him. Investing a high pick in that position could set up the defense really well, and if Chris Cole is gone early in the first, trading back for Kyngstonn Viliamu-Asa would be a great move. Viliamu-Asa can play throughout the defense, is an incredible run defender, is very athletic, and is a tackling machine. He has dealt with injuries and can be a target in the passing game, which is why he won’t be a higher pick, but at the back of the first round, he could be a really good option.

title: If Saints win/lose vs. Bears
summary: The New Orleans Saints are on the road again when they face the Chicago Bears in Week 11 on Sunday. Here’s what either result could mean for the black and gold. If the Saints win: A win would be one of the shocks of the week across the NFL. Odds makers give the Saints little […]
full_text: The New Orleans Saints are on the road again when they face the Chicago Bears in Week 11 on Sunday. Here’s what either result could mean for the black and gold. If the Saints win: A win would be one of the shocks of the week across the NFL. Odds makers give the Saints little chance; they’re coming off a home game in which they blew a huge opportunity to somewhat grab a hold of the division. Despite returning closer to full health at key positions, Kellen Moore’s squad continues to squander chances to win games. In Chicago, there will be no room for error. If the Saints can pull it off, it drags them straight back into the playoff picture and would certainly mark a statement victory. If the Saints lose: A defeat to Chicago wouldn’t come as a surprise to many, and it would be another step toward missing the playoffs in the weak NFC South. It feels as though New Orleans doesn’t have to be where they are. But even if they were nearer or above .500 right now, this is still a game that would be chalked up as a loss in a lot of fans’ eyes. Should the Saints continue to drift away from the division lead, it won’t be the Bears game that got them there, but the ones that have come before. Do you give the Saints a chance to pull it off in Chicago? Let us know in the comments!

(Photo by Geoff Stellfox/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 3-6 New Orleans Saints are headed to the Windy City this weekend to take on the Chicago Bears at Soldier Field. It’s a matchup in which few are giving the Saints a chance to win, but New Orleans is on a mission looking to silence the doubters and pull off a major upset on the road. Chicago enters Sunday’s contest with an impressive 7-2 record, riding a four-game winning streak and are coming off a bye week. The Bears have emerged as one of the NFC’s stronger teams, averaging nearly 27 points per game. They have been dominant on defense, particularly on third down, making it difficult for opposing offenses to sustain drives. For the Saints, coming off a disappointing home loss to the Carolina Panthers, the challenge will be getting points on the board early and finding consistency on both sides of the football while limiting costly mistakes against a strong Chicago team. PREDICTION: BEARS 38 – SAINTS 24 Unfortunately, the Bears have the bigger talent, momentum and home-field advantage which will likely freeze out the Saints of any chance of getting a victory in Chicago. title: Our Defense vs. Their Offense: Chicago Bears
summary: The Chicago Bears and head coach Ben Johnson will be bringing the 7th-ranked offense in the NFL with them when they play the New Orleans Saints on Sunday. The Bears may have a young, budding superstar QB in Caleb Williams, but they are a ball-control, run-dominant offense. The Bears lead the league in time of […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LA - NOVEMBER 15: Cameron Jordan #94 of the New Orleans Saints celebrates with Kaden Elliss #55 after a sack against the Carolina Panthers during the second half of a game at Caesars Superdome on November 15, 2026, in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Derick Hingle/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Chicago Bears and head coach Ben Johnson will be bringing the 7th-ranked offense in the NFL with them when they play the New Orleans Saints on Sunday. The Bears may have a young, budding superstar QB in Caleb Williams, but they are a ball-control, run-dominant offense. The Bears lead the league in time of possession at 34:31 and rushing attempts with 303, and they average over 4 yards per rush. They are second in the NFL with 17 rushing TDs. The efficiency of this offense does not stop there. They are in the top 5 in rushing yards, averaging 142 yards per game, and third-down conversions at 45.3%. As dynamic as Caleb Williams is as a QB, the passing offense has not been highlight-reel explosive. That does not mean Williams cannot make those types of plays, but Johnson has done a very good job this year of keeping the offense on schedule, and Williams is creating when he needs to. The passing offense ranks 12th in the NFL, averaging 241 yards per game. They only have 10 passing TDs so far this season. Part of the reason for this is that Williams was unable to play for three weeks due to a hamstring injury. He has not missed a game since returning against Atlanta, and the Bears have not lost since his return. The Saints are bringing one of the worst defensive units in the league to Soldier Field on Sunday. The Saints’ defense will have to enter this game with the mentality that they cannot allow Chicago to run the ball. This is easier said than done because the Saints are 27th in rushing defense, allowing 129 yards per game on the ground. The advantage the Saints will have is when the Bears drop back to pass. The Saints have 26 sacks on the season so far and are tied for 9th in the NFL. If they can force Williams to throw the ball and keep him contained within the pocket, they will have a chance to cause negative plays. The Saints’ defense will have to be opportunistic and create chaos in the backfield for Chicago. Williams is getting better, but he also has 5 interceptions on the season with only 8 TDs. Can the Saints make him feel uncomfortable and force him to give the ball up? The Saints will have to slow down D’Andre Swift and Kyle Monangai. This running back combination has accounted for over 900 rushing yards on 215 carries and 13 rushing touchdowns. This further stresses the importance of forcing the Bears into third-and-long situations and obvious passing downs so the edge rushers and Kaden Elliss can play to their strengths. The Saints will look to shock the NFL and hand the Bears their third loss of the year. Do you think the Saints’ defense can stop the Bears’ offense?

title: College Football Week 12: Three draft prospects to watch for the NY Giants
summary: Good morning New York Giants fans! Happy Saturday and welcome to Week 12 of the college football season. The college football playoff picture is starting to come into focus, and we’re seeing some truly surprising teams enter the Top 12. Much as we didn’t expect Indiana or Miami to make the runs they did last […]
full_text: ﻿UCLA running back Wayne Knight carries the ball | ISI Photos via Getty Images Good morning New York Giants fans! Happy Saturday and welcome to Week 12 of the college football season. The college football playoff picture is starting to come into focus, and we’re seeing some truly surprising teams enter the Top 12. Much as we didn’t expect Indiana or Miami to make the runs they did last year, so too have teams like Utah, Wake Forest, and UCLA surprised us. As usual, we’re using the NFL Draft as a lens through which to look at both college football and the state of the Giants. We’ll be spotlighting players who could fill potential needs on the Giants’ roster come draft time — and today that’s wide receiver, running back, and cornerback. Georgia Tech vs. (11) Wake Forest ESPN – noon Player spotlight: Carlos Hernandez (WR, Wake Forest) No, that isn’t a typo, the Demon Decons are 11th in the country and should make the College Football Playoffs. And one of the biggest engines driving their rise up the rankings has been wide receiver Carlos Hernandez. The 6-foot, 190 pound senior has emerged as one of the most prolific wideouts in the country. So far this year he’s hauled in 67 catches for 1,039 yards, and 8 touchdowns. Hernandez might not have blazing speed, but he’s a detailed route runner who has excellent start-stop quickness and explosiveness out of his breaks. He reminds of Victor Cruz with a thick lower body, great contact balance, and a tendency to turn into a running back after making the catch. It’s easy to see him turning into an instant star in the right situation. Michigan vs. (4) UCLA CBS – 3:30 p.m. Player spotlight: Wayne Knight (RB, UCLA) I wouldn’t blame anyone for watching the game between Tennessee and LSU instead of this one, but I also didn’t want to wait longer to spotlight UCLA running back Wayne Knight. Knight isn’t getting the national attention of backs like Jadan Baugh or Kewan Lacey, but he has been one of the country’s best runners since QB Nico Iamaleava was lost for the season. Knight is a compact sparkplug of a back at 5-foot-7, 200 pounds with great vision and patience behind the line of scrimmage to go with his natural leverage, quickness, and contact balance. He excels at pressing his blocks, using his size to hide behind offensive linemen, then exploding through holes to pick up yardage. His short legs not only make him hard to tackle, but also give him great stride frequency that make for great acceleration and quickness. And while he might not look it, Knight is both a tenacious short-yardage back and fast enough to outrun the athletic Oregon defense. (21) South Carolina vs. (1) Georgia ABC – 7:30 p.m. Player spotlight: Vicari Swain (CB, South Carolina) Sitting here, I believe that the Giants should extend Deonte Banks, at least locking up their starting corners for the next few seasons. And while the Giants just drafted Colton Hood out of Tennessee, they could look to draft another in the first two days to maintain their depth at the position if they move on from Paulson Adebo. Swain is a classic “South Carolina” corner with solid size (6-foot, 195 pounds), fluid hips, a physical demeanor, and the upside to be a sticky press-man corner. He also has a good nose for the ball with 9 passes defensed, 3 interceptions, and 2 forced fumbles over the last two seasons. All of that fits well in Dennard Wilson’s defense. But what could really put him over the top in the eyes of John Harbaugh is his special teams upside. Swain serves as one of South Carolina’s primary punt returners and currently leads the SEC in punt return yardage. He’s averaged 14.4 yards per return over the last two years and has 5 punt return touchdowns since the start of last season. He led the SEC in return touchdowns last year with 3 and currently leads the conference with 2 return touchdowns. Returner has been a revolving door for the Giants, and finding a reserve corner, with starting upside, who is also a potential weapon as a returner could be very attractive.

title: NY Giants’ pass defense has been much better than expected
summary: There were, if not outright concerns, certainly questions about how good the New York Giants defense could be in 2026. Between edge defenders Brian Burns, Abdul Carter, and Kayvon Thibodeaux, as well as off-ball linebackers Tremaine Edmunds, Arvell Reese, and Micah McFadden, the Giants’ linebacking corps was expected to be one of the best in […]
full_text: New York Giants defensive back Jevon Holland and Deonte Banks celebrate after an interception. | Getty Images There were, if not outright concerns, certainly questions about how good the New York Giants defense could be in 2026. Between edge defenders Brian Burns, Abdul Carter, and Kayvon Thibodeaux, as well as off-ball linebackers Tremaine Edmunds, Arvell Reese, and Micah McFadden, the Giants’ linebacking corps was expected to be one of the best in the NFL. And the hope was that their defensive line would at least be serviceable after the addition of veteran defensive tackles D.J. Reader and Shelby Harris. The bigger questions were about the Giants’ secondary, particularly after Cor’Dale Flott left in free agency. 2025 free agents Paulson Adebo and Jevon Holland hadn’t panned out in their first years as Giants, while 2023 first round pick Deonte Banks had regressed badly under DC Shane Bowen and was considered a bust. The Giants signed former Cleveland Browns and Jacksonville Jaguars cornerback Greg Newsome II, as well as former Baltimore Ravens safety Ar’Darius Washington, in the 2026 free agency period and drafted Tennessee cornerback Colton Hood in the second round of the draft. However, those moves weren’t viewed as much more than Band-Aids for a Giants’ secondary, and national commentors suggested that the Giants’ scondary could be putrid in the first year of John Harbaugh’s rebuild. Fast-forward nine games, and the Giants’ secondary has been much, much , better than anticipated under Dennard Wilson, Donald D’Alesio, and Addison Lynch. The Giants are currently fielding the NFL’s fourth-best defense in total yardage allowed (2,751 total yards). They’re third-best in passing yardage allowed per game (184.1 yards per game), second in yards per completion allowed (9.8 yards per completion), and 2nd in yards per attempt allowed (6.2 yards per attempt). The Giants are accomplishing this feat with smothering coverage from their starting corners. Both Deonte Banks and Greg Newsome II have been incredibly sticky in man coverage, allowing little separation for receivers. CB Separation Prevented & On Ball Grade pic.twitter.com/Ur1AAOquwB — Jrfortgang (@throwthedamball) November 20, 2026 Banks is allowing just 2.1 yards of separation as the nearest defender, per NFL NextGenStats, while Newsome is allowing all of 2.6 yards of separation. Banks and Newsome are both forcing tight window throws on over 40 percent of the plays in which they’re the closest defender — which is exactly what the “step coverage” Dennard Wilson’s defense calls for. ( note: “step coverage” calls for the defensive back to be within a step of the offensive player ) And while slot corner Dru Phillips is allowing more separation (3.6 yards on average), he’s allowing -5.9 EPA in coverage and a Catch Rate Over Expected of -13.0 percent. Defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson praised the Giants’ safeties when he spoke to the media on Thursday, saying, “I think Ar’Darius played his best game the last outing against Washington. Obviously, he tackled extremely well. You saw him, in the fourth quarter in a critical situation, come up with an interception. He’s been doing everything that I know he could do, from being around him in Baltimore when he was there. He is a smaller guy that plays with a big stick. He is going to attack the line of scrimmage. He tackles well. He can cover. So he’s doing a good job. I think all the safeties are doing a good job in their role. It’s kind of safety by committee. All of them deserve the opportunity to play. So that’s why we’ve been playing them.” And Wilson wasn’t just puffing up his players. Each of the Giants’ safeties have played very well in coverage as well. Safety Separation Prevented & On Ball Grade pic.twitter.com/zWzZKQYicC — Jrfortgang (@throwthedamball) November 20, 2026 Jevon Holland has been among the best safeties in the NFL this year, allowing a -27.8 percent catch rate over expected which is 3rd best among all DBs in the NFL and -13.4 EPA allowed. Jason Pinnock has proven to be remarkably sticky in coverage The Giants’ airtight coverage is allowing them to lead the NFL in the rate of Cover-0, that is man coverage across the board, at 10.8%. That jumps to 11.8% in obvious passing situations, and the Giants are sixth in EPA allowed in those situations. Expected pass situations (EP >=70% based on down, distance, score, time left, etc) pic.twitter.com/pbLv2o08KD — Football Insights 📊 (@fball_insights) November 17, 2026 Interestingly, the Giants’ pressure rate has been remarkably low when only rushing four defenders, even with their sticky coverage. That’s led to frustrations from fans when it comes to sack totals (or the lack thereof), particularly with regard to Abdul Carter and Kayvon Thibodeaux. Both of the Giants’ starting EDGEs have elite get-offs, but have all of 2.0 sacks between them. NextGenStats has shown us that part of the problem is that the Giants’ opponents specifically game plan for their hyper-athletic pass rushers. The Giants’ opponents feature the second-fastest Time To Throw of any defense in the NFL, as well as a Top-3 deviation from their usual Time To Throw. How does each defense influence Time to Throw? Opposing offenses get the ball out in an average of 2.74s against the Jaguars defense (4th fastest), but that’s 0.17s quicker than they typically do against all other defenses (largest reduction in NFL). pic.twitter.com/8L8Bm4r7ls — Doug Analytics (@Doug_Analytics) November 19, 2026 The Giants’ sticky Cover-0 packages work with Wilson’s aggressive blitz patterns (as he refers to them) to provide an answer. The Giants are now second only to the Minnesota Vikings — and the madman that is Brian Flores — in the average number of pass rushers sent at 4.90. Average number of pass rushers by pre-snap alignment Dennard Wilson sneaking into Brian Flores territory pic.twitter.com/9xrjqHLDwz — Doug Analytics (@Doug_Analytics) November 19, 2026 The Giants are currently sitting at 5-3-1 on the season, and they can thank their defense for closing out four of those wins, as well as forcing the tie against the Washington Commanders. All told, the Giants’ secondary has been one of the most surprising units in the entire NFL, and it’s powering a defense that is finally playing up to its potential. I suspect they’d be getting much more attention on the national level it weren’t for the low sack numbers and what Flores is doing in Minnesota. Now, the Giants will need them to keep it up, or perhaps even find another level if they can.

title: New York Giants mailbag: Play calling, Malik Nabers, Dominic Zvada, more
summary: Ben Fitzsimmons asks: I know Matt Nagy is the OC and is the one calling plays. I don’t fully understand how Greg Roman fits into it. We’ve seen the Giants run it between the tackles at least 400 million times on first down this year. We’ve seen that terrible play from the infamous JJ Package […]
full_text: Ben Fitzsimmons asks: I know Matt Nagy is the OC and is the one calling plays. I don’t fully understand how Greg Roman fits into it. We’ve seen the Giants run it between the tackles at least 400 million times on first down this year. We’ve seen that terrible play from the infamous JJ Package show up a few times (still hasn’t worked once btw). We’ve seen the Giants attempt and fail miserably to run the clock out at the end of games multiple times this year. We’ve seen a lack of creativity in the run game as they mostly just run behind Ricard and hope it works (it usually doesn’t). What I’m curious about is how much of that is Greg Roman and how much is Matt Nagy. Is Roman designing the run plays and Matt Nagy is just calling them? Is Roman just providing advice and vibes while Nagy draws up the plays? Does Roman have any impact on how run plays are called each game (I would assume not, but I’ve been wrong many times before)? Ed says: Ben, Greg Roman’s title is ‘Senior Offensive Assistant’. Nagy runs the offense and makes all play-calling decisions. He makes final determination, with John Harbaugh’s input, on the game plan. Roman is acknowledged as one of the best run-game designers in the game today. To my knowledge, Roman is responsible for designing much of the Giants’ run game. Harbaugh has explained that much of the vertical passing game comes from Nagy’s background. As I’ve said, Roman’s specialty is the run game. Nagy’s job, as he has explained it, is to take the menu of options he has in front of him and decide what to use and when to use it. Roman, who has been an offensive coordinator multiple times, sits in the booth with Nagy on game days. Of course there will be some sharing of information and ideas. The decisions, though, are Nagy’s to make. We see the warts. Sometimes, you make the wrong call. Sometimes, you make the right one and players don’t execute it. The Giants are 14th in the league in score at 22.6 points per game. That’s pretty good, considering that they are on their third quarterback and have struggled mightily to block in the run game. Bob Donnelly asks: Following the Commanders’ game you have questioned some of the offensive play calls, especially not running the ball in a few key situations. The OC makes the play call yet much of the blame/criticism seems to be directed towards the HC and his lack of confidence in his team’s ability to run the ball in those situations. In your view how much play calling influence does our head coach exert in critical situations? Ed says: Bob, the reality is that the head coach gets credit when things go right, and everything that goes wrong also lands at his feet. Harbaugh does not call the plays. He can set the direction, though. Does he want the ball run? Thrown? What personnel does he want in the game. Tom Donlan asks: Malik Nabers can make spectacular catches and carry the passing game with a high volume of targets and catches. We’ve also seen drops and a costly fumble against Washington, as well as what some view as immature or disruptive behavior with poor body language on the field. What do you think he needs to do to become a more consistent No. 1 receiver, and do you know how the Giants view the way he voices his frustrations publicly? Ed says: Tom, Malik Nabers has a drop rate this season of 3.5%, per Pro Football Reference. That isn’t exactly terrible. He has fumbled three times in 185 career touches, one basically every 62 touches. Again, that isn’t awful. Drops happen occasionally. No one who has the ball a lot goes through a career without fumbling at times. I’m not getting into the body language debate. As far as becoming a more consistent No. 1 receiver, how about getting some consistent reps with the quarterback. Nabers barely had any time with Jaxson Dart last year. Nabers’ reps were limited all summer as he came back from his knee injury, then Dart went down for the season in Week 2. Now, Nabers and J.J. McCarthy have worked together for a month. My educated guess is the Giants would like him to choose his words more carefully. But, he was encouraged to speak his mind freely as a rookie, and he is still a 23-year-old kid learning to grow up with a much different coach than the one who drafted him. One other thing I will say is that I still believe Nabers has to learn to do a better job fighting to protect his quarteerback. I’m thinking about that interception at the end of the Washington game. The receiver simply has to put up a fight there to make sure the ball gets knocked down and not intercepted. Joel Story asks: I read an article saying that after the Giants/Eagles game on Nov. 8th, Kayvon Thibodeaux was fined $11,941 for taunting, Jeremiah Trotter was fined $6,428 for tripping, Zack Baun was fined $6,750 for illegal use of the helmet, and Andrew Mukuba was fined $9,041 for a hit on a defenseless player. Are these amounts correct? If so, do you know why the NFL/NFLPA have chosen to fine players more for taunting than for the other three actions which could potentially end other players’ seasons or even their careers? Ed says: Joel, yes those amounts are correct. The fine schedule, which you can see it for yourself , is collectively bargained. Taj Siddiqi asks: JH is being criticized for keeping Dominic Zvada and let Jason Sanders walk. Sanders is performing like a pro while Zvada is struggling. Some people think one of the causes for his firing at Baltimore was his decision to stay with the kicker, whose name I can’t recall. Is JH over confident regarding his ability to evaluate kickers? Is the guy at the Baltimore still there or is he even in the league? Ed says: Taj, John Harbaugh has been around long enough to fully understand the ups and downs, and the risks, of choosing to ride with a rookie placekicker. Harbaugh had a rookie placekicker in Baltimore last season. Tyler Loop was very good for the Ravens in 2025. He made 30 of 34 field goals (88.2%). Harbaugh got fired because the Ravens missed the playoffs and the organization felt like his tenure had run its course after 18 years. It just so happens that Loop missed a 44-yard field goal on the final play of that game that would have gotten Baltimore into the playoffs. It was his only miss of the year between 40 and 49 yards. How does anyone criticize a coach for riding with a kicker who went 30 of 34? Loop is still with the Ravens, but he is injured and on IR. Overconfident in his ability to evaluate kickers? Well, he and the Ravens drafted Jordan Stout in the fourth round in 2022. Stout is probably the best punter in the league. Sam Koch punted in Baltimore for 16 years, 14 of those for Harbaugh. Justin Tucker was the best field goal kicker in the NFL for more than a decade, and was bombing 60+ yard kicks long before there were a bunch of other kickers in the league capable of doing it. I would say Harbaugh knows good kickers when he sees them. If Harbaugh ends up being wrong about Zvada, that will be the first kicker or punter he has been wrong about in his time as a head coach. As for Jason Sanders, I saw a number of those practices in the spring. A day or two before he got cut I watched him try to kick a 50-ish yard field goal on a windy day, and I watched the ball basically die and go straight down a couple yards short. I didn’t think he could handle the MetLife Stadium conditions, either. Francis Castros asks: Can you provide the rehabilitation status of the following players and are they required to rehab at the Quest Diagnostics Training Center? – Tyrone Tracy Jr. — RB (Hamstring) – Tremaine Edmunds — LB / MLB (Chest / Shoulder) – Braxton Berrios — WR (Foot – surgery) – Chauncey Golston — DE / Edge (Neck) – Jaxson Dart — QB (Knee – Meniscus) – Brian Burns — LB (Knee – ACL) – Roy Robertson-Harris — DE (Achilles) – Calvin Austin III — WR (Knee) – Rico Payton — CB (Undisclosed) – Jarrick Bernard-Converse — CB (Knee) – Gunner Olszewski — WR (Achilles) – Thaddeus Dixon — CB (Achilles) Ed says: Francis, I…
