title: Drew Lock or Sam Darnold: Who gives the Seahawks the best chance to win?
summary: The Seattle Seahawks enter their bye week facing a decision that could define the rest of their season. Sam Darnold is expected to return from injury, but Drew Lock has done more than enough to make the quarterback conversation interesting. Lock is 3-0 in games he has started and has appeared in four victories this […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks enter their bye week facing a decision that could define the rest of their season. Sam Darnold is expected to return from injury , but Drew Lock has done more than enough to make the quarterback conversation interesting. Lock is 3-0 in games he has started and has appeared in four victories this season. Across those appearances, he has completed 68 of 93 passes (73.1%) for 837 yards, seven touchdowns and zero interceptions. He has also posted a 125.6 passer rating. Darnold, meanwhile, is 2-4 in his six full starts, with 1,478 passing yards, 10 touchdowns, nine interceptions and a 79.5 passer rating. The numbers make a compelling case for Lock. But there is more to this discussion than the stat sheet. The quality of the defenses they faced, the support provided by the running game and, perhaps most importantly, the type of football Brian Fleury wants his offense to play all matter. The numbers favor Drew Lock, but context matters There is no denying that Lock has been efficient. His 73.1% completion rate, seven touchdowns and zero interceptions are impressive, especially considering he has taken five sacks for 31 yards lost. His 125.6 passer rating is also considerably higher than Darnold’s 79.5. Darnold, on the other hand, has struggled to protect the football. Nine interceptions in six full starts is a significant problem, particularly for a team that wants to build its identity around a strong defense. He has also taken 17 sacks, losing 113 yards in the process. Lock has been more efficient, more careful with the football, and better at avoiding negative plays. Still, the sample size is considerably smaller, and the circumstances surrounding their performances have been very different. The quality of competition matters The biggest argument in Darnold’s favor is the quality of the defenses he has faced. Lock’s four appearances came against the Patriots, Cardinals twice, and Raiders. Arizona and Las Vegas have been among the league’s worst scoring defenses, while New England has been closer to the middle of the pack. Darnold, meanwhile, had a much tougher stretch. His six full starts came against Washington, the Chargers, 49ers, Broncos, Chiefs, and Bears. San Francisco, Denver, Kansas City and Chicago have all presented considerably more difficult defensive challenges than the Cardinals and Raiders. That is a meaningful difference. Lock has taken advantage of favorable matchups, while Darnold has had to deal with considerably tougher defenses. This doesn’t mean Lock’s production should be dismissed. He can only play the teams on Seattle’s schedule, and he has consistently given the Seahawks a chance to win. But comparing their raw numbers without considering the quality of the defenses they faced would be unfair. The running game hasn’t provided the same support One of the biggest differences between the two quarterbacks has been the support they have received from the running game. During Drew Lock’s four victories, Seattle’s running backs (excluding quarterback rushing) produced 472 yards on the ground, averaging 118 yards per game and 4.2 yards per carry. They also scored four touchdowns. During Sam Darnold’s four losses, the running backs managed just 260 yards, averaging 65 yards per game and 3.2 yards per carry. They scored only two touchdowns. That’s a substantial difference. Lock has benefited from a ground game that has been more productive, allowing Seattle to control the pace, stay ahead of the chains and avoid putting too much pressure on its quarterback. But the quality of the defenses they faced makes this comparison even more interesting. Darnold faced run defenses that ranked, on average something near to the 12th in the NFL. His six opponents ranked second, seventh, 10th, 13th, 19th and 24th against the run. Lock’s four opponents, meanwhile, ranked an average of 25th. Their run defenses ranked 14th, 28th, 28th and 31st. In other words, Darnold faced considerably tougher run defenses and still had to deal with a running game that averaged just 65 yards per game in his four losses. Lock had a much more favorable set of matchups and received significantly better production from his running backs. Against Washington, he threw for 379 yards and four touchdowns, while the running backs combined for just 39 yards on 17 carries. He wasn’t the reason Seattle’s offense struggled in that game. He was practically the entire offense. Ultimately, the running game has been a major advantage during Lock’s victories and a significant weakness during Darnold’s losses. That context should be part of any fair evaluation of their performances. Lock’s conservative approach might fit Fleury’s offense better This might be the most important argument in favor of giving Lock the starting job. Darnold probably has a higher ceiling. When everything clicks, he can make throws and create plays that Lock might not be capable of consistently reproducing. His best football is probably better than Lock’s best football. But the other side of that argument is just as important: Darnold’s worst performances can be considerably more damaging than Lock’s. Turnovers have been a recurring problem throughout Darnold’s career. Even during his strong stretches last season, there were moments when questionable decisions threatened to undo the good things he was doing. This season, that tendency has become increasingly difficult to ignore. Lock, at least in this current season, has played a more conservative brand of football. He has taken what defenses give him, avoided forcing throws into coverage and allowed the rest of the team to do its job. That approach could be a better fit for what Brian Fleury is trying to build offensively, especially with a defense capable of keeping games competitive. The Seahawks don’t necessarily need their quarterback to win games by himself. They need someone who can avoid putting the defense in difficult situations, protect the football and take advantage of scoring opportunities. Lock has done exactly that so far. I don’t know if Lock has the talent to win the games Darnold has lost. But Darnold’s turnovers have probably made some of the games Seattle won much more difficult than they needed to be. That is an important part of this discussion, too. This decision could define Seattle’s season There is another important consideration: Seattle might not have the luxury of changing quarterbacks again. At 6-4, the Seahawks are approaching a critical stretch of their season. Their next game against the San Francisco 49ers could determine whether they remain in contention for the NFC West title. More importantly, every loss from this point forward could seriously jeopardize their chances of making the playoffs. That’s why whoever starts against San Francisco will probably remain the starter for the rest of the season, or at least for as long as Seattle still has a realistic path to the postseason. If the Seahawks find themselves needing to change quarterbacks again after that game, it will probably mean they have already lost more games and put their playoff hopes in great danger. There would be little point in continuing to experiment with the position at that stage. This is ultimately what makes the decision so important for Mike Macdonald during the bye week. He isn’t choosing a quarterback for one game. He may be choosing the player who will lead Seattle through the most important stretch of its season. Macdonald has publicly maintained that Darnold remains the team’s starting quarterback when healthy. That suggests he is still the preferred option, and it is entirely possible that his health, rather than a decision to bench him, will determine who starts against San Francisco. But Lock has made this decision much less straightforward. Seattle doesn’t necessarily need someone capable of making spectacular plays every week. It needs someone who can keep the offense functional, protect the football and avoid turning…

title: Seahawks restructure Sam Darnold, Julian Love, and Ernest Jones contracts
summary: The Seattle Seahawks may have the week off, but they have been busy working the financial books to free up some salary cap space in recent days. OverTheCap, which reviews all NFL contracts, revealed on Friday that the Seahawks restructured three star players, all of whom are impending free agents at the end of the […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks may have the week off, but they have been busy working the financial books to free up some salary cap space in recent days. OverTheCap , which reviews all NFL contracts, revealed on Friday that the Seahawks restructured three star players, all of whom are impending free agents at the end of the 2027 season. The Seahawks created $9.88 million in cap room with simple restructures of the contracts of Sam Darnold, Julian Love and Ernest Jones. https://t.co/4T7wF6Xv7e — Jason_OTC (@Jason_OTC) November 20, 2026 What do those restructures look like? Let’s consult the notes! Void years aplenty to help spread out future cap charges. Sam Darnold The Seahawks converted $5.5 million of salary into a bonus and added an additional void year for salary cap purposes. The move reduced Darnold’s 2026 salary cap number by $4.4 million and increased his future cap numbers by $1.1 million in each season. Ernest Jones IV Seattle added three void years and converted $3.342 million of salary to a bonus to create $2.674 million in cap room for 2026. His future cap increases by $668,500 per year. Julian Love The Seahawks converted $3.51 million of salary to a bonus and added three void years for cap purposes in 2026. The move created $2. million in cap room for the year while adding $702K in charges to each remaining season. There’s a typo in Love’s contract notes, but presumably the restructure created about $2.8 million in cap room just to the three totals add up to $9.88 million. Seattle has over $13 million in cap space, which has led to obvious speculation about working on an extension for Quenton Nelson, or even a cheaper one for Zach Charbonnet, both of whom are impending free agents in just a few months. They could also be looking ahead to other extensions in 2027, which include when Byron Murphy II is eligible for a new contract. As far as how the restructure affects Darnold, he is due a $10 million roster bonus in March. Cutting or trading him after June 1 would be very feasible and save over $38 million in cap space , otherwise not a ton has really changed in terms of figuring out his future beyond 2027. But something’s happening here. What it is ain’t exactly clear.

title: Puka Nacua won’t play vs. Seahawks after ‘likely’ season-ending MCL surgery
summary: After Thursday’s news that Los Angeles Rams star receiver Puka Nacua’s league-imposed 3-game suspension would be served while on injured reserve, it turns out Nacua’s next game will probably be in the 2027 season anyway. Rams head coach Sean McVay said on Friday that Nacua, who was placed on IR following MCL and PCL sprains […]
full_text: After Thursday’s news that Los Angeles Rams star receiver Puka Nacua’s league-imposed 3-game suspension would be served while on injured reserve , it turns out Nacua’s next game will probably be in the 2027 season anyway. Rams head coach Sean McVay said on Friday that Nacua, who was placed on IR following MCL and PCL sprains (plus turf toe), will undergo what is likely season-ending knee surgery. Rams star WR Puka Nacua will undergo MCL surgery and is likely going to miss the rest of the season. He'll be out "a couple months," per Sean McVay. — Nate Atkins (@NateAtkins_) November 20, 2026 Nacua sustained the injury on a very needless 3rd and 11 handoff when trying to run the clock out against the Washington Commanders. Keep in mind that Nacua was already targeted 19 times and caught 14 passes in this game, in addition to taking a handoff earlier in the contest. All-Pro WR Puka Nacua suffered a knee injury on the Rams’ final offensive snap today, and will undergo an MRI on Monday to determine the extent of the injury, per @MikeGarafolo and me. The team does not believe he suffered a torn ACL, but the imaging Monday will tell more. pic.twitter.com/S264w2Fe0A — Adam Schefter (@AdamSchefter) November 8, 2026 The surgery news obviously means that, barring one hell of an overestimation of his recovery timeline, Nacua will not play against the Seattle Seahawks in Weeks 16 or 18, which could be critical matchups as far as making the playoffs. Davante Adams should be back within the next few weeks after rupturing his hamstring, but if he’s not back any time soon then the Rams could go into upcoming games against the Green Bay packers, Kansas City Chiefs, and San Francisco 49ers without their top two receivers, not to mention injuries to offensive linemen Steve Avila and Coleman Shelton. LA’s dream superteam is steadily falling apart, and there’s no guarantee at this point that the Christmas Day showdown at Lumen Field will even have playoff implications for the Rams at this stage. Their fate may actually come down to their defense and the Myles Garrett/Aaron Donald combo to step up in the face of a likely passing offense dropoff.

title: 7 former Seahawks chosen in the 2027 UFL Draft
summary: The 2027 UFL Draft wrapped up Thursday, with six players who previously spent time with the Seattle Seahawks selected across the 15-round event. The group includes a former seventh-round NFL draft pick, a former fifth-round Los Angeles Rams selection, several undrafted free agents and players who spent time with Seattle during training camp or on […]
full_text: The 2027 UFL Draft wrapped up Thursday, with six players who previously spent time with the Seattle Seahawks selected across the 15-round event. The group includes a former seventh-round NFL draft pick, a former fifth-round Los Angeles Rams selection, several undrafted free agents and players who spent time with Seattle during training camp or on the practice squad. Not all of them appeared in a regular-season game for the Seahawks, but each had a connection to the organization. Here is a closer look at their time in Seattle and where they are headed next. Marvin Jones Jr. – Dallas Renegades Edge rusher | No. 11 overall | Second round Jones joined Seattle as an undrafted free agent in May 2026 after finishing his college career at Oklahoma. He spent time with the team during the offseason and eventually earned another opportunity on the practice squad in August. His second stint didn’t last long, as Seattle released him on September 5. Dallas made Jones one of its earliest selections, taking him 11th overall in the second round. Derrick Graham – St. Louis Battlehawks Offensive tackle | No. 13 overall | Second round Graham’s time in Seattle was brief. The Tulane offensive tackle originally signed with the Houston Texans as an undrafted free agent in June 2026. After leaving Houston, he received an opportunity with the Seahawks. Seattle signed him on August 25, but released him just four days later. He never made it to a regular-season game with the team. Jalan Gaines – Orlando Storm Edge rusher | No. 14 overall | Second round Gaines joined Seattle as an undrafted free agent in May 2025 after playing at Illinois State. He quickly made an impression during his first preseason game against the Las Vegas Raiders. With the game tied 23-23 and time expiring, Gaines blocked Daniel Carlson’s 55-yard field goal attempt , preserving the tie and denying Pete Carroll a victory in his return to Lumen Field. That wasn’t his only encouraging moment. Gaines continued to flash during training camp, showing some pass-rush ability and the kind of athleticism that made him an intriguing developmental prospect. He eventually spent time on the practice squad before signing a future contract with Seattle in February 2026. The Seahawks gave him another opportunity, but he couldn’t secure a permanent roster spot. Chris Paul Jr. – Dallas Renegades Linebacker | No. 18 overall | Third round Paul Jr. arrived in Seattle with an interesting background. The Los Angeles Rams selected him in the fifth round of the 2025 NFL Draft, 172nd overall, before waiving him. The former Ole Miss linebacker had a strong final college season, recording 88 tackles, 11 tackles for loss and 3.5 sacks in 2024. He earned All-American recognition and was a Butkus Award finalist. There was reason to believe Paul could develop into a useful NFL linebacker. He joined Seattle in 2026 and showed some of that potential during the preseason. His best performance came against the Tennessee Titans in Week 2 of this year. Paul recorded eight total tackles, six of them solo, and added a tackle for loss. He was one of Seattle’s more productive defensive players that night. Unfortunately, his opportunity came to an abrupt end. Paul was waived with an injury designation on August 27, following the Titans game. He never got the chance to establish himself in Seattle’s regular-season defense. J.R. Singleton – Orlando Storm Defensive tackle | No. 46 overall | Sixth round Singleton joined Seattle as an undrafted free agent after the 2025 NFL Draft, coming out of Iowa State. He spent time with the Seahawks during training camp and the preseason, showing flashes as an interior defensive lineman. His ability to compete along the defensive front made him an interesting developmental option, even if he wasn’t able to turn those moments into a permanent roster spot. Seattle continued to give him opportunities during its offseason roster-building process, but Singleton ultimately couldn’t establish himself as a long-term option. Damien Martinez – Colorado Stampede Running back | No. 60 overall | Eighth round Martinez is probably the most recognizable name on this list for Seahawks fans. Seattle selected the RB with the 223rd overall pick in the seventh round of the 2025 NFL Draft. Martinez entered the league after a productive college career at Oregon State and Miami, finishing his final season with 1,002 rushing yards and 10 touchdowns. He entered training camp competing for a place in Seattle’s running back room but couldn’t secure a spot on the initial 53-man roster. The Seahawks brought him back on the practice squad after roster cuts. His time in Seattle eventually came to an end, and he was most recently with the Green Bay Packers practice squad. Brenden Rice – Colorado Stampede Wide receiver | 84th overall pick | 11th round Brenden Rice is another notable name on this list. The son of legendary wide receiver Jerry Rice, who also played for Seattle late in his career, Brenden began his professional journey after being selected by the Los Angeles Chargers in the fifth round of the 2024 NFL Draft. He appeared in three games during his rookie season, primarily contributing on special teams, before ending the year on injured reserve. The Chargers released him in August 2025, and he subsequently spent time on the New England Patriots’ practice squad. The Seahawks signed Rice to their practice squad on November 18, 2025. His time in Seattle was short-lived, however, as the team released him on December 2 without appearing in a regular-season game. Rice will now get another opportunity with the Colorado Stampede. Other former Seahawks already in the UFL The seven players selected in the 2027 UFL Draft aren’t the only former Seahawks looking to continue their football careers in spring football. Several other players with Seattle ties are already on UFL rosters for the upcoming season. Here are some additional names worth keeping an eye on. Colorado Stampede (3) Mike Novitsky, C: Novitsky signed with Seattle as an undrafted free agent in 2024 out of Kansas. He spent time on the practice squad and signed a future contract before being released in April 2025. Raiqwon O’Neal, OT: O’Neal had multiple stints with Seattle, including time on the active roster in 2023 and the practice squad in 2024. The Seahawks originally acquired him after he spent time with Tampa Bay. Cam Bright, LB: An undrafted free agent out of Washington in 2023, Bright spent part of the offseason with Seattle before being released. St. Louis Battlehawks (1) Sal Cannella, TE: Cannella signed with Seattle in August 2023 after an impressive season with the XFL’s Arlington Renegades. His stay with the Seahawks lasted just six days, but he went on to establish himself as one of spring football’s more productive tight ends. He has earned All-UFL recognition and is now back with St. Louis. Columbus Aviators (2) Easop Winston Jr., WR: Winston spent time with Seattle in 2023 and was part of the Seahawks’ initial 53-man roster. He also returned to the organization on a future contract and was part of the practice squad. Walter Palmore, DT: Palmore spent time with Seattle during the 2021 offseason after signing in May. He also had opportunities with other NFL teams before building a career in spring football. He’s been in spring football since 2022. Dallas Renegades (2) Jalen McKenzie, OL: McKenzie spent time on Seattle’s practice squad in 2022 and signed a future contract with the Seahawks in January 2023. He later moved on to other NFL organizations before joining the UFL. The former Ole Miss and UCF quarterback was also an intriguing athlete because of his ability to contribute at quarterback and receiver. Those will show up this week with Christian McCaffrey 1-on-1 in the open field, or Keenan Allen settling into the vacated area of a blitzer, or George Kittle and Deebo Samuel keeping the offense ahead of the chains on a screen pass.” Kyle Shanahan shares final updates ahead of 49ers-Vikings “I think it’s pretty easy just because of, it’s definitely easy for the coaches just because of what our schedule’s like. If the 49ers’ defense can hold Minnesota under that, they’ll get to 9-1 and on to a big home game against Seattle next weekend.” Five vital 49ers to watch vs. Vikings in Mexico City as NFC powerhouses collide “Minnesota blitzes on 78.6 percent of pass plays. That is nearly 30 percent higher than the next closest team in the NFL. But the Vikings don’t save their blitzes for just passing situations. They will test the 49ers on all downs, and San Francisco cannot afford any plays in which their offensive line is confused on their individual assignments.” The Cowboys might be ‘America’s Team.’ The 49ers aim to become the world’s team (paywall) “Offensive lineman Isaac Alarcon is from Monterrey, Mexico, while defensive tackle Sebastian Valdez’s parents were born in Mexico. He said an aunt, uncle and cousins will be at the stadium to cheer for him Sunday. “I grew up in San Diego, but I went to TJ (Tijuana) all the time,” he said. “And it just means a lot to my family and me to be able to represent my ethnicity, my culture and just show people it’s possible.” ….Their experience Down Under was so impressive that the 49ers are considering applying for marketing rights in Australia through the league’s Global Markets Program. They are also interested in expanding their footprint in Asian markets. The NFL has had to scuttle previous attempts to play games in China, but it remains on its radar, York said. He also noted the 49ers have played preseason games in Japan three times (1989, 1995 and 2002) and said, “I know Japan would like to have us back again.” “There’s some real interest in the NFL in the Philippines,” he added. “I don’t know if I can tell you that that’s the hottest next market, but we’re looking to do something in Asia.” 49ers’ Mike Evans on track to play vs. Vikings after missing past month with Achilles injury (paywall) “The 49ers will have a walk-through practice at the Air Force Academy on Saturday morning before departing for Mexico.” ‘It felt like a calling’: How 49ers’ Christian McCaffrey is fighting for veterans (paywall) “His foundation’s flagship initiative provides medical and mental-health care for Special Operations forces veterans suffering from post-traumatic stress. The program is run in conjunction with Resilience Code, whose founder, Dr. Chad Prusmack, has worked with McCaffrey for more than a decade on his athletic performance and cognitive function. title: Where the 49ers need to improve defensively vs. Vikings
summary: Last weekend was not a good day for the San Francisco 49ers defense, as they gave up 40 points on the Dallas Cowboys, yet still managed to come away with the 46-40 victory. San Francisco’s defense struggled on all fronts. The secondary especially had its issues, as Dallas’s top three receivers all had quality games. […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TEXAS - NOVEMBER 15: Nick Bosa #97 of the San Francisco 49ers rushes the passer during a game against the Dallas Cowboys at AT&T Stadium on November 15, 2026 in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Stacy Revere/Getty Images) | Getty Images Last weekend was not a good day for the San Francisco 49ers defense, as they gave up 40 points on the Dallas Cowboys, yet still managed to come away with the 46-40 victory. San Francisco’s defense struggled on all fronts. The secondary especially had its issues, as Dallas’s top three receivers all had quality games. George Pickens had 11 catches for 145 yards and three touchdowns, and that was with him dropping three passes. CeeDee Lamb had seven catches for 72 yards and a touchdown, while Ryan Flournoy had six catches for 71 yards and a touchdown. Cornerbacks Deommodore Lenoir, Renardo Green, and Upton Stout entered the game banged up, and it showed, as both had their fair share of struggles against Dallas’s elite offense. Of course, the matchup wasn’t easy facing a high-caliber quarterback with two Pro Bowl receivers, but it was a rough day for a defense that had been quite good over the first half of the season. That wasn’t the only issue. The 49ers pass rush was also ineffective, failing to sack Dak Prescott, and Nick Bosa came out this week and took accountability for his play this season. Bosa has yet to record a sack, although his other numbers still indicate a productive season, especially with the double teams and chips he’s facing. Now, this week, the health is looking better. Stout remained limited in practice with his ongoing shoulder injury and is questionable, but Lenoir wasn’t on the injury report and Renardo Green practiced in full on Thursday and is off the injury report for Sunday’s game. But the 49ers still have a tough challenge against the Minnesota Vikings, who put up 30 points on the Green Bay Packers in Kirk Cousins’s return. Minnesota’s offense suddenly looks formidable, and this battle should be a tough one on both sides. After their struggles against Dallas, where do the 49ers need to improve defensively against Minnesota? Ahead of Sunday night, defensive coordinator Raheem Morris broke down the main issues he saw from the Cowboys game and what to take from it. “Extending drives early with some of the penalties to get those guys to go down there, particularly on the first drive [was a problem]. We gave up three, I believe, on that first one,” Morris said. “We got the big penalty to get those guys down there. They got a big-time field goal kicker. A couple of big plays in the first half. The two big plays were the ones that killed us there early. Got a pretty good grip on it after that and kind of held it down. It was at some point it was like 38-19. Then that finishing moments, we didn’t do a very good job of getting the finishes off. Usually, the finishes happen when you’re able to generate pressure with sacks or you’re able to get interceptions. “The Cowboys did a nice job, to give them credit, of getting the ball out of their hand. Did a nice job of getting the ball into their good players’ hand, keeping drives going, extending drives. They had about three or four drives there where it was almost like overtime-like play for them, where it was going to be fourth down territory regardless and they were able to capitalize and go down and score on us. You would like to be able to stop some of those plays and be able to get those guys going and get off the grass at those moments and then that score wouldn’t have got to where it was, but those things didn’t happen. “We didn’t execute that way. And it’s a collective group. I know [Nick] Bosa stood up in front of you guys and took all the credit and took all the accountability, but I really think it’s just all of us. Some of it could be better play calls for them. Some of it could be better for us, what we can do for those guys. Some of it can be better plays made by us. Some of it, we just ran out a little bit of gas, got a little bit tired. Let’s not kid ourselves. Human nature as well. So, fortunate to get out of there with a win. Definitely want to learn those lessons when you get a chance to do those things in those moments, when you get wins. Something that we can learn from and grow from and something that we definitely will.” One thing Morris did see from his team was accountability after the game, with the leaders on the team stepping up. “They’re such an accountable group,” Morris added. “Most guys, you come in and you’re just upset after a game. These guys, they hold themselves to such a high standard. They come in, they’re able to speak very clearly right off the bat. So it’s not going to be more vocal the next week because they were vocal the first week. Not necessarily Bosa. Bosa’s kind of a to-himself guy, but for a guy like Fred [Warner], he’s always going to speak up and do the things that happened. It wasn’t like there was mistakes. They did some better job executing. There was a few mistakes. There’s always going to be mistakes and there’s always correcting mistakes. I’m not saying there’s not mistakes, but there’s always going to be correcting mistakes, but you correct those mistakes, you move on. “There’s some other things that, just you talking to as an individual player. The best thing about our guys, they always point at themselves first. Whether it’s Fred, whether it’s Bosa, whether it’s DMo (Deommodore Lenoir), Renardo [Green], anybody on our football team. That’s the cool part about being here with these guys is they point at themselves first. Then a lot of the times I’m able to say, ‘Hey, I can help you here’ or ‘we can do these things better. We can make these calls. We can help you out, do a little bit better in these situations.’ They are all so upfront and forthgoing with those things. That makes it really cool to talk to those guys that way.” Health seemed to be a factor last weekend, but the 49ers do need to be more disciplined and avoid the killer penalties (although some looked to be questionable calls). But there is a lot at stake this weekend for the 49ers, as their No. 1 seed odds shift dramatically with a win or a loss. San Francisco’s offense has always been up to the task, but they’ll get their toughest matchup of the year with Brian Flores’s defense. So, the 49ers defense will need to show up as well against this new-look Vikings offense with Kirk Cousins and execute on all three levels.
author: Rohan Chakravarthi

title: The one matchup that will tip 49ers-Vikings: Dallas Turner versus Trent Williams
summary: Sunday night is a huge game for the San Francisco 49ers and the Minnesota Vikings. The winner will likely be in the driver’s seat for the number one seed in the NFC with a tiebreaker over the other team. Now, there is no way to predict what will happen down the stretch, but this game […]
full_text: (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images Sunday night is a huge game for the San Francisco 49ers and the Minnesota Vikings. The winner will likely be in the driver’s seat for the number one seed in the NFC with a tiebreaker over the other team. Now, there is no way to predict what will happen down the stretch, but this game feels like a playoff game and, for many, not all, the marbles. The must-see matchup is clearly Kyle Shanahan against Brian Flores. Interesting subplots include Kirk Cousins facing the 49ers again and Jauan Jennings returning to face his old team. One matchup deserves a closer look and could tip the scales for both teams. EDGE rusher Dallas Turner is in the mix for DPOY and rightfully so. However, Will Anderson IV might have a stranglehold after last night’s performance. Everyone is all over Flores’ blitz rates and the exotic nature of his coverages, but Turner has completely broken out in 2026. The 23-year-old has a bright future ahead of him in the NFL. On the other side of the age spectrum, there stands 38-year-old Trent Williams. Sunday will be the first time the two will do battle. Turner lines up everywhere, which is to be expected in Flores’ scheme. The right side is where he has his highest snap numbers, with 253 snaps between RE and REO. Colton McKivitz will draw Turner also, but Williams will likely see Turner more. According to PFF, Turner has generated 45 pressures, which is the sixth-most among qualified EDGE rushers. On 305 pass-blocking snaps in 2026, Williams has allowed one sack, two QB hits, five hurries, and eight pressures. Against two of the more ferocious pass rushes in Seattle and Denver, Williams posted back-to-back clean sheets. Communication for the offensive line will be paramount on Sunday night as Flores will send the house more often than not, and many Vikings defensive linemen and rushers benefit from the confusion and chaos caused by Flores, but Turner vs. Williams is a matchup the 49ers have to win. Sunday will be filled with plenty of star power, and Turner will have his impact, but against Williams, he must be turned away and shut out. This is the classic case of “old guard” vs. “new guard.” Regardless of your fandom, Sunday night is the best matchup of the weekend and possibly the season so far. Grab your popcorn, and watching two of the best in the business will be a delight for all.
author: Jason Aponte

title: Why Sunday night’s game vs. the Vikings could be the most important one of the season
summary: Sitting in first place in the NFC, the San Francisco 49ers look to be facing their toughest battle yet in Week 11, as they take on the Minnesota Vikings in primetime in Mexico City. San Francisco had an outstanding offensive performance last weekend against the Dallas Cowboys, out-dueling their counterparts 46-40 to improve to 8-1, […]
full_text: San Francisco 49ers wide receiver Deebo Samuel Sr. scores a touchdown against the Dallas Cowboys during the first quarter on Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026, at AT&T Stadium in Arlington, Texas. (Amanda McCoy/Fort Worth Star-Telegram/Tribune News Service via Getty Images) Sitting in first place in the NFC, the San Francisco 49ers look to be facing their toughest battle yet in Week 11, as they take on the Minnesota Vikings in primetime in Mexico City. San Francisco had an outstanding offensive performance last weekend against the Dallas Cowboys, out-dueling their counterparts 46-40 to improve to 8-1, tied for the best record in the NFL. However, their ailing defense struggled in a big way against one of the more talented offenses in the league. Now, they get a completely different challenge on Sunday night, taking on the league’s best defense and best defensive coordinator with the highest stakes on the line: the NFC’s No. 1 seed. The 49ers are in the midst of their toughest stretch of the year. They just played the Cowboys, get the Vikings this week, and then get the Seattle Seahawks, New York Giants, and Los Angeles Rams, all potential playoff contenders, in the weeks after. So, keeping their lead for the No. 1 seed is paramount, which means a win on Sunday is a top priority. Now normally, I’d vote for divisional games to be the most important ones for the 49ers, as nothing tops taking care of business in the tough NFC West. But Sunday’s game against the Vikings could actually be the most important one of the season for the 49ers, as there are serious implications with the No. 1 seed on the line. If the 49ers win on Sunday, ESPN’s Aaron Schatz, the creator of DVOA, projects San Francisco to have an 81 percent chance of getting the No. 1 seed in the NFC. Should they lose? That number falls all the way to 26 percent in Schatz’s simulations, with the Vikings jumping from five percent to 51 percent for the No. 1 seed. Now, the 49ers are still the team with the second-highest odds to win the Super Bowl on FanDuel at +550, behind the Buffalo Bills at +500. They also currently have the best odds to win the NFC (+250), with the Vikings (+470) second. We’ll see how major that change is pending this weekend’s outcome. With the current state of the NFC West and how strong the 49ers have started the season, making the playoffs doesn’t seem to be in jeopardy. The 49ers have -700 odds to win the NFC West, and FanDuel gives them -110 odds to win over 13.5 games this season. But having the No. 1 seed would be huge for January, as the playoffs would run through San Francisco, giving them the best chance at making the Super Bowl in a very wide-open race this season. San Francisco does get a strong end to its schedule. Three of their last four will be against the Los Angeles Chargers, Philadelphia Eagles, and Arizona Cardinals. But they have to weather the storm in the coming weeks with a couple of matchups against playoff hopefuls, starting with Sunday night against the Vikings. Minnesota looked rejuvenated last weekend, beating the Green Bay Packers 30-10 on the road in Kirk Cousins’s first start back. The 49ers just saw Cousins two weeks ago, and they’ll have their hands full on both sides of the ball. Heading into the game, San Francisco is a 3-point favorite over Minnesota, and they’ve got a ton at stake in the heavyweight NFC battle.
author: Rohan Chakravarthi

title: 49ers final injury report: Mike Evans is ‘going in the right direction’
summary: San Francisco 49ers head coach Kyle Shanahan spoke about the final injury report on Friday. The team did not rule out any of the 53-man roster. There are nine players with questionable designations: WR Mike Evans (Achilles)LB Dre Greenlaw (neck)CB Upton Stout (shoulder)RB Jordan James (calf)DT CJ West (knee)CB Nate Hobbs (adductor)DE Khalid Kareem (ankle)QB […]
full_text: (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images San Francisco 49ers head coach Kyle Shanahan spoke about the final injury report on Friday. The team did not rule out any of the 53-man roster. There are nine players with questionable designations: WR Mike Evans (Achilles) LB Dre Greenlaw (neck) CB Upton Stout (shoulder) RB Jordan James (calf) DT CJ West (knee) CB Nate Hobbs (adductor) DE Khalid Kareem (ankle) QB Mac Jones (illness) LB Luke Gifford (chest) When asked about his first day of practice on Thursday, Shanahan said, “He had a good day of practice yesterday. As always, he’s a little sore today, but going in the right direction.” Shanahan said the team will see how Evans does during Saturday’s walkthrough before deciding his game status. When asked how much of a difference Evans makes, Shanahan said: “I think the guys have done a good job of holding it down without Mike out there. Mike’s our guy. A very unique player. Been doing it at a high level for a very long time. Played really well in the games he played this year. Be great to get him back.” The 49ers practiced at half speed on Friday, according to Shanahan. If that’s the case, and knowing that Saturday is a walkthrough, it’d be a surprise if Evans wasn’t in uniform this Sunday night. Earlier in the month, Shanahan said they felt Evans could have played if the circumstances were different. After disposing of the Raiders and Cowboys, the next month’s schedule will feature four consecutive teams jockeying for playoff position. On Dre Greenlaw, Shanahan said, “Hoping he’ll be alright. You never know with nerves and neck and stuff. But hoping it continues to go in the right direction.” Starting cornerbacks Renardo Green and Deommodore Lenoir are doing “a lot better” and are off the injury report. “Good. They didn’t practice last week and weren’t sure if they were going to fully play, and they’re not on the injury report this week, so a lot better.” We’ve seen the other team’s biggest pass-catching threat have a field day against the secondary in two straight games. Justin Jefferson is probably licking his chops after what he’s seen in the past couple of games. The 49ers need to decide whether cornerback Nate Hobbs or defensive tackle CJ West can improve their roster. Their 21-day practice window closes on December 2. If the Niners don’t activate either player by Wednesday, the season is over for Hobbs and West. The Hobbs signing was always strange, because he’s never been the type of player who played on special teams. He didn’t hold up on the perimeter at cornerback, so he became a slot by necessity. He’s a veteran, but it’s unclear where he’d help the secondary. On Mac Jones feeling better: “I believe so. I think he’s trying to get out there today.”

title: How the 49ers are uniquely equipped to beat the Vikings
summary: The Week 11 NFL slate leaves a lot to be desired. Two games on the schedule involve playoff teams. The big one is an international outing between the Minnesota Vikings and the San Francisco 49ers. The Vikings saw their season circling the drain, so they traded for a familiar face in Kirk Cousins. Nobody was […]
full_text: Photo by Brian Rothmuller/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Week 11 NFL slate leaves a lot to be desired. Two games on the schedule involve playoff teams. The big one is an international outing between the Minnesota Vikings and the San Francisco 49ers. The Vikings saw their season circling the drain, so they traded for a familiar face in Kirk Cousins. Nobody was happier with the trade than Justin Jefferson, who caught a season-high nine passes in Cousins’ debut last week. Missed opportunities defined Raheem Morris’s stop unit last week, as he explained . The Niners defense will look to bounce back after a game in which they finished in the 6th percentile in points allowed per drive. The other side of the ball features two of the very best at what they do. The mad scientist Brian Flores boasts one of the most impressive defenses we’ve seen through 10 weeks. Minnesota bottled up a high-powered Lions offense, kept the Bills in check, and turned Jordan Love and the Packers offense into a pumpkin last week. The only team to slow down the 49ers offense this year is themselves. They’ve scored 30+ points five times this season, including a season-high 46 last week against the Cowboys. Big plays were the name of the game for San Francisco, as they were in the 99th percentile in EPA per play against Dallas. The biggest edge in this game is on special teams. Minnesota ranks first in schedule-adjusted efficiency, while the Niners rank 29th. The Vikings are fifth or better in field goals, kickoff return, punt return, and are sixth in hidden points. The 49ers are smack dab in the middle at 16th in hidden points, largely because of their punter. But it shouldn’t surprise anyone to see the punt return unit rank second-to-last, or the field goal team come in at 28th. The third phase of the game is generally what decides these one-possession contests. Let’s dig deeper into each offense and defense to see how this game could play out. What to expect when the 49ers are on defense Contrary to what you might have seen online leading up to this game, the 49ers defense and Vikings offense do exist. Flores and Shanahan are not the only play-callers in this game. Pump the brakes on Kirk Cousins’ debut The Vikings scored 30 against the Packers, so the initial thought might be that Kirk Cousins was all that was needed to jumpstart an offense that has been dormant all year. After going three-and-out and losing a yard to start the game, the Vikings drove from Green Bay’s 10-yard line. They lost six yards and settled for a field goal. On the next drive, the Vikings had another short field after the Packers missed a field goal. Myles Price caught a 38-yard touchdown on 3rd and 23 on a play that should have never resulted in a completion. After going three-and-out on their ensuing drive, Cousins threw an interception in the red zone, but his knee was down. On 3rd and 15, Green Bay was in press man coverage with no safety help, and gave up 24 yards. Minnesota scored on the next play. Thirty points. One drive that was legit. Zooming out, the Vikings had an EPA per play in the 54th percentile, a success rate in the 52nd percentile, and a yards per play in the 28th percentile. Cousins was money on third downs, which flipped the variance in the Vikings’ favor. Rancid run game Functionally, the Vikings struggle to run the rock. Minnesota is running more gap and man concepts than ever under Kevin O’Connell, which may explain some of the struggles. Despite ranking fifth in the league in yards before contact, Minnesota is 25th in rushing success rate and 29th in EPA per rush. They had a 12-yard run last week on a pitch to a wide receiver. Aaron Jones shook free for a 19-yard run. But he only averaged 4.3 yards per carry. Their rushing leader, old friend Jordan Mason, had 16 carries but managed just 3.7 yards per carry. It’s easy to chalk up a subpar run game to poor quarterback play, but the Vikings are 27th in team rush yards over expectation (- 73) and 21st in 10+ yard rushes. I’ve always appreciated Mason for being a tough, hard-nosed runner. What the Niners do well is exactly how you keep Mason under wraps. All the slanting and stunting the defensive line does will force Mason to redirect. That’s what you want. If you let Mason pick up some steam, he’ll pick up 5-7 yards, easily. But if you make him change directions, he turns into a mediocre back. It’s tough to use 5-down fronts against a wide-open offense like the Cowboys, who live three wide receiver sets. Minnesota uses 11 personnel nearly 40% less than Dallas. O’Connell uses two tight end sets 27.7% of the time, the 9th-highest rate in the league, and runs plays from under center at the sixth-highest clip. Against 5-down fronts last week, the Vikings had 15 carries and averaged 3.8 yards. I’d expect Raheem Morris to deploy more 5-down fronts than usual, especially on early downs, to keep the Vikings in longer down-and-distance situations. It also means more Jaden Dugger, which is a good thing, who only played 11 snaps last week. Something smells about the Vikings’ run game. The 49ers have to win this facet of the game. The defense has allowed five rushes of 10+ yards this season, far and away the best in the league (second place has allowed 16). They’re second in rushing EPA on the season. Minnesota’s offensive line is far from a bully ball unit. Their tight ends aren’t effective in the run game, which could lead to multiple negatives to force obvious passing downs. They ask 180-pound receivers to block in the fit, and the results are as you’d imagine. This is the type of game where you notice Nick Bosa and Mykel Williams control the line of scrimmage. Jettisoning Jettas Christmas came early for Justin Jefferson last week. He saw a season-high 13 targets. Kyler Murray acts like it’s against the rules to throw the ball over the middle, which is why Jefferson has only nine targets in the middle third this season. His 49 yards are tied for 146th in the NFL, per Next Gen Stats. That’ll change with Cousins, who has the second-most yards this season over the middle of the field. The Packers tried to bracket Jefferson at times last week, but to no avail. Credit Cousins for throwing the ball on time before the double team could get there. But the Packers had opportunities for turnovers on Jefferson targets. They dropped an interception. You’ll live with the underneath throws, like the curls and the screens—but you better make a tackle and limit the damage after the catch. What you have to take away are the deep over routes or any kind of crossing route. You’re not going to shut down a focal point of the offense like Jefferson. However, you can eliminate throwing zones schematically and ensure he doesn’t beat you over the top. Fred Warner has erased the middle of the field this entire decade. Teams simply do not target the intermediate part of the field with No. 54 on the field. Dak Prescott had 51 attempts in Week 10. Six of those were beyond 10 yards over the middle. Warner lurking in that area should impact how the Vikings want to attack San Francisco. If Price or Felton beat you, then so be it. There isn’t a George Pickens at WR2 for Minnesota. The 49ers are much better equipped to slow down this unit than they were last week. What to expect when the 49ers are on offense The most impressive part about Brian Flores is his ability to dictate what an offense does. He makes coordinators tuck their tails and get out of what they want to do offensively. He speeds up quarterbacks with the blitz, but limits their options because extra blockers have to stay in and protect the pass. Flores’ scheme takes immense pressure off his coverage unit, while creating 1-on-1s across the board for his pass rush. It’s fascinating to watch. The 49ers are built to win the math against Brian Flores Last week, the Packers had five eligible receivers run a route on 33.7% of their dropbacks. It felt like Jordan Love left a…
author: Kyle Posey

title: 3 areas where the Vikings can offset the 49ers’ strengths
summary: I mean, Sunday night will be everything football is all about. A primetime fight between two of the best teams in the NFC, one featuring the most high-powered offense while the other features the most-feared defense in the league, as the 8-1 San Francisco 49ers host the 7-2 Minnesota Vikings on Sunday night at the […]
full_text: (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images I mean, Sunday night will be everything football is all about. A primetime fight between two of the best teams in the NFC, one featuring the most high-powered offense while the other features the most-feared defense in the league, as the 8-1 San Francisco 49ers host the 7-2 Minnesota Vikings on Sunday night at the 49ers’ second home away from home: Estadio Azteca in Mexico City. It’s been a few years, but the last time the 49ers made the trip down to Mexico City, they destroyed the Arizona Cardinals 31-14 on a Monday night. But the Vikings will be a much tougher test than that Arizona team was, being a team the 49ers haven’t defeated since 2021 (and most notably since Brian Flore became Minnesota’s defensive coordinator). In the two games Kyle Shanahan has taken on a Minnesota defense led by Flores, the 49ers are 0-2 while averaging 17 points per in the pair of games. And while there’s plenty to talk about on the other side of the ball (Kirk Cousins, Justin Jefferson, and Jauan Jennings, just to name a few), this week’s numbers will focus on the marquee matchup of Sunday night: the 49ers offense against the Vikings defense: 14.0 Points per game. The Minnesota defense allows 14.0 points per game, best in the league. Two touchdowns. That’s the average game for the Vikings defense. The 49ers have scored at least 14 points by halftime in seven of their nine games this season. And while the 49ers are among the best-scoring teams in the league, Minnesota has shown it’s more than capable of slowing down some of the better offenses in the league. Of Minnesota’s nine games, seven have come against teams that enter Week 11 in the top half of points per game. Minnesota allowed: 22 points to Green Bay in Week 1 (13 th in points per game) 3 points to Chicago in Week 2 (7 th ) 16 points to Tampa Bay in Week 3 (15 th ) 13 points to New Orleans in Week 5 (16 th ) 19 points to Detroit in Week 8 (6 th ) 23 points to Buffalo in Week 9 (1 st ) 10 points to Green Bay in Week 10 That’s an average of 15.1 points per game against top-half offenses. The game listed above that maybe to pay close attention to is the Week 9 game against Buffalo. The Bills are the only team to average more points per game this season than the 49ers. Entering Week 9, the fewest points Buffalo had scored was the 24 it had scored in Week 3 against the Chargers and next to that the 26 points scored the next week against New England. Other than that, the Bills have scored more than 30 points in the other six games. Minnesota held them to 23 points. The 49ers are similar, as they have scored 30 or more in five of their nine games, while only once were the 49ers held to fewer than 23 points, which also just so happens to be the 49ers’ only loss. But it’s not just the Bills: the Packers, Bears, and Lions can all say they have had their lowest scoring output this season against the Vikings. And only the Packers, in one of their two matchups against Minnesota, can say they were chasing a Kirk Cousins-led offense. San Francisco has been held to less than 14 points just once over its last 26 regular season games, but if anybody can slow down this version of the 49ers’ offense, it would be this version of the Vikings defense. 25.0 Red zone scoring percentage. The Vikings’ defense has allowed a touchdown on 25.0 percent of red zone trips, the best red zone defense in the NFL. Oh look, another thing that San Francisco’s offense is good at doing that could potentially be canceled out by Minnesota’s defense. San Francisco is one of the more prolific red zone offenses in the league, ranking fourth in the league in red zone touchdowns (24) with the highest red zone scoring percentage in the league (82.8 percent), despite ranking 17 th in red zone attempts (29). Minnesota’s defense neither allows opposing offenses into the red zone, or on the rare occasion they do, don’t allow teams to score touchdowns in the final-fifth of the field. While Minnesota is tied at the top with the Giants defense with only 20 red zone entries allowed, the Vikings have allowed by far the fewest red zone touchdowns with five (compared to the Giants’ 16 red zone touchdowns allowed). Three-fourths of the time a team enters the red zone, teams score three points or fewer. Only once this season have the 49ers faced a defense in the same stratosphere as the Vikings in terms of red zone attempts allowed, and that was back in Week 5 against Seattle. Entering Week 11, the Seahawks have allowed the third-fewest red zone entries in the league at 23. That didn’t seem to bother the 49ers, however, as San Francisco scored a touchdown on all three red zone attempts in that game. But that’s the thing: while Seattle is good at not allowing teams into the red zone, once teams enter, Seattle doesn’t stop them from scoring, allowing a touchdown on 16 of 23 red zone drives. San Francisco has already done well against a team that doesn’t allow a lot of red zone entries but does allow plenty of red zone touchdowns. Against Minnesota, it will be just as much of an issue scoring from inside the red zone as it is entering it. 67.3 Blitz percentage. Minnesota blitzes on 67.3 percent of opposing drop backs, the top rate in the league. This has been one of my favorite stats to track throughout the season because of how ridiculous it is. Two-thirds of the time, Minnesota sends an extra rusher, which is a whopping 23 percent higher than how much the Vikings blitzed in 2025. To put it in the context of the 2026 season, the New York Giants currently sit second behind the Vikings in blitz rate, blitzing on 37.5 percent, which means Minnesota is blitzing at a 29.8 percent higher rate than the second-place Giants. That difference is more than the difference between the G-Men and the last-place Cincinnati Bengals, who blitz at a 16.8 percent rate, a difference of 20.7 percent. There really is no way to contextualize just how much the Vikings blitz compared to everybody else. So, it’s tough to think about how the 49ers offensive line will handle the frequency of pressure Flores’ Vikings defense will put on the San Francisco front. Only two of the nine games the 49ers have played so far this season have come against teams entering Week 11 in the top-ten of blitz rate, and that was Week 4 against Denver and Week 6 against Washington. But even then, that comparison isn’t apt, as Denver’s blitz rate of 31.2 combined with Washington’s 35.7 rate falls 0.4 percent short of Minnesota’s blitz percentage. Just to record-keep, the 49ers allowed two sacks combined against Washington and Denver but can’t feel very comfortable heading into Vikings week after allowing five sacks to a Cowboys defense that ranks 29 th in blitz rate and ninth in pressure rate (unsurprisingly, Minnesota ranks first in pressure rate as well). The 49ers offense is as good as anybody’s, but no there’s no defense in the NFL quite like Brian Flores’ Minnesota Vikings’ defense.
author: Andrew Pasquini

title: Out of the Den: Nick Bosa has been here before, and Sunday is Week 3
summary: There’s a stretch every spring when the most dangerous animal in the woods is still half asleep. Scientists have a name for it: walking hibernation. For two to three weeks after it leaves the den, the animal is on its feet, but its body is still on winter time. It moves stiffly and slowly. It […]
full_text: (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) There’s a stretch every spring when the most dangerous animal in the woods is still half asleep. Scientists have a name for it: walking hibernation. For two to three weeks after it leaves the den, the animal is on its feet, but its body is still on winter time. It moves stiffly and slowly. It stays close to home. But it hasn’t lost an ounce of what makes it dangerous. The muscle is all still there. It just doesn’t move like it yet. Then, all at once, the woods remember what lives there. Nick Bosa walked back into the light in Week 9. Sunday night in Mexico City is his third game back. He’s been here before This is the third time Bosa has torn an ACL. The first was Oct. 30, 2015, his senior year at St. Thomas Aquinas. Right knee. His season was over before the playoffs. His dad, John, said the family was “sick about it 24 hours a day.” Two months into rehab, Nick said something that sounds a lot like him: “I think I’ll be the same player for sure.” He had five sacks as a freshman at Ohio State. The next year, he was the Big Ten’s Defensive Lineman of the Year. The second was Week 2 of 2020, against the Jets. Left knee. He told Richard Sherman later that during that rehab he “felt like there was no light at the end of the tunnel.” Then he came back in 2021 with 15.5 sacks and a league-high 21 tackles for loss. Even then, he said his knee “kind of improved throughout the entire season.” That’s the pattern. He always comes back. It just takes time. The third winter The third was Week 3 of last season, against Arizona. Right knee again. “These surgeries are big-time traumas, physically and mentally,” he said this summer. Then, two games into his return, a calf injury cost him five more. So for all the noise, Bosa has played four games this season. Read the numbers, and you can tell the ground hasn’t thawed. His pressure rate is 12.5%, the lowest of his career. His get-off, how quickly he’s moving after the snap, is 0.85 seconds. In 2024, it was 0.70. In this building, that number is gospel. Kris Kocurek has coached the 49ers’ defensive line since 2019, and everything in his room starts at the snap. Ever since, the soundtrack of a 49ers practice has been one man and four words: GTFO. And that 0.70 in 2024 was the quickest of Bosa’s career. Fifteen hundredths of a second is about a step, and the first step is always the last thing to wake up. Offenses still plan like the muscle never left, because it didn’t. He’s seeing a chip or a double team on 32.3% of his rushes, the most of his career. And the 49ers get pressure on 35.4% of dropbacks with Bosa on the field and 29.8% without him. “I don’t think I’m playing my best football right now,” he said Wednesday. A plan built for a full appetite Here’s the part that matters for Sunday. While Bosa was out, Raheem Morris got creative. Through Week 8, the 49ers lined up five men on the line on 43.1% of snaps, more than they had in any of Kyle Shanahan’s previous nine seasons. Those five-man looks have produced pressure 38.2% of the time, up from 31.1% last year. Then Bosa came back, DeForest Buckner came home, and the 49ers went back to rushing four. In their first game together, the five-man front fell to 21.3%. Over the first seven games, they sent five or more on 31.5% of dropbacks. In the two games since, it’s 20.9%. The four haven’t gotten there. Over the last four weeks, the 49ers have turned one of 31 pressures into a sack, the lowest rate in the league. The rest of the front has spent the week in Colorado getting loose. On Tuesday, six defensive linemen, Buckner included, went fly fishing on the Arkansas River. Their guide summed it up: “The fish don’t care who you are.” Neither does Kirk Cousins. He gets sacked on just 11.1% of his pressures, the second-lowest rate in football. He gets rid of it before anything with claws can get there. And an animal on tender feet doesn’t take the long way around. Tim Ryan, who rushed the passer in this league, said on KNBR this week that he’d like to see “fewer games and more straight rushes,” fewer stunts and more one-on-ones, and to “let these dogs eat.” Give Bosa the same tackle over and over until he finds the move that wins. John Lynch said he expects Bosa to start “impacting games starting this week in a big way.” Walking hibernation lasts two to three weeks. Sunday is week three. And even a groggy animal can still find full speed when something gets close enough. And November is when bears eat.

title: Brock Purdy is ticking two historically significant boxes for MVP
summary: Brock Purdy faces arguably the biggest test of his MVP credentials this Sunday in Mexico City when the 49ers face the Minnesota Vikings. The Vikings have been a thorn in Purdy’s side both times he has faced them in his career. Indeed, Brian Flores’ defense has been the puzzle Purdy has yet to figure out, […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TEXAS - NOVEMBER 15: Brock Purdy #13 of the San Francisco 49ers looks to pass during the second half against the Dallas Cowboys at AT&T Stadium on November 15, 2026 in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Stacy Revere/Getty Images) | Getty Images Brock Purdy faces arguably the biggest test of his MVP credentials this Sunday in Mexico City when the 49ers face the Minnesota Vikings. The Vikings have been a thorn in Purdy’s side both times he has faced them in his career. Indeed, Brian Flores’ defense has been the puzzle Purdy has yet to figure out, with San Francisco’s signal-caller completing over 74 percent of his passes but throwing three interceptions and also losing a fumble across two defeats to Minnesota. And the challenge that lies ahead of Purdy at Estadio Azteca is a formidable one, as the Vikings’ ultra-aggressive defense leads the NFL by EPA per play and success rate, Minnesota allowing a successful offensive play just 37.8 percent of the time. Should he overcome it and record his first win over the Vikings to solidify the 49ers’ stranglehold on the NFC by improving to 9-1, Purdy’s MVP case will be significantly strengthened. However, the numbers suggest he is already ticking two important statistical boxes with his performances through the first nine games of the season, albeit three other quarterbacks are doing the same. Per Sumer Sports, nine of the last 10 players to win MVP had a EPA per play average of 0.159 or more, and a win rate of at least 68.8 percent. With the 49ers at 8-1 and Purdy comfortably leading the NFL with an EPA per play of 0.313, the San Francisco signal-caller is meeting both criteria with little difficulty. The problem is that three AFC quarterbacks operating at the top of their game — Josh Allen, Joe Burrow and Trevor Lawrence — are also checking both boxes through 10 weeks of the season. MVP prediction datapoints, updated to include Wk 10 https://t.co/8GdTBIyo3k pic.twitter.com/yhjqc07fFc — Lindsay Rhodes (@lindsay_rhodes) November 16, 2026 As such, despite his extraordinary level of play so far this campaign, Purdy will need to do plenty more to separate himself from a group of players who might have been viewed as more obvious MVP candidates going into the season. The best way to do that is by delivering more signature performances in high-profile games. Purdy’s standout display to this point is his effort in leading the 49ers on a game-winning drive on the road against the Seattle Seahawks in Week 6, while his superb show of playmaking ability in last week’s shootout win over the Dallas Cowboys will also have helped his cause. But it will be the stretch run that decides whether he becomes the 49ers’ first MVP since Steve Young in 1994. Strong performances will be required against Vikings, in the return meetings with the Seahawks and Los Angeles Rams, and in a mouthwatering road game with the Kansas City Chiefs in Week 16. Deliver in that set of fixtures, and it will be difficult to dispute Purdy’s case, and confidence in him as an MVP candidate and in the 49ers as the class of the league should increase significantly if he can pass the Flores test on Sunday.

full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - NOVEMBER 15: Cam Ward #1 of the Tennessee Titans warms up prior to the game against the Jacksonville Jaguars at Nissan Stadium on November 15, 2026 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Johnnie Izquierdo/Getty Images) | Getty Images For the first time in years, fantasy football people are touting a Tennessee Titans quarterback. Cam Ward has been playing better over the last month, and the Titans are facing a Dallas Cowboys pass defense that has gotten lit up in recent weeks. The stars are aligned for a big game from Ward. title: 3 Titans players should dominate vs. Cowboys in Week 11
summary: The Tennessee Titans made an offensive shift over the previous three games. They’ve prioritized the development of sophomore quarterback Cam Ward by calling a pass-happy, no-huddle offense. The results have been extremely encouraging. The Titans are averaging nearly 30 points per game on offense since letting Ward execute his preferred approach. On Sunday, they’ll play […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OHIO - NOVEMBER 01: Cam Ward #1 of the Tennessee Titans looks on against the Cincinnati Bengals during the first quarter at Paycor Stadium on November 01, 2026 in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Photo by Andy Lyons/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Tennessee Titans made an offensive shift over the previous three games . They’ve prioritized the development of sophomore quarterback Cam Ward by calling a pass-happy, no-huddle offense. The results have been extremely encouraging. The Titans are averaging nearly 30 points per game on offense since letting Ward execute his preferred approach. On Sunday, they’ll play against a Dallas Cowboys defense allowing 28.2 points per contest. The following Titans players should thrive in Sunday’s Week 11 matchup . QB Cam Ward Cam Ward is arguably playing the best football of his career right now (certainly of his sophomore season). His 28 completions versus the Jaguars tied a previous career high, and his 71.8% completion percentage was a season-best result. In the previous game, Ward had his first-ever 300 yard passing performance against the Bengals. He’ll look to keep the momentum rolling versus a struggling Cowboys defense. WR Carnell Tate Carnell Tate is returning to the lineup after a two-game absence with a shoulder injury. In one appearance since the Titans made notable changes on offense, he recorded five catches for 69 yards against the Browns. With Ward currently playing admirably, getting Tate back into the lineup should have another positive effect on a surging offense. The rookie fourth overall selection could dominate the Cowboys’ undermanned secondary. RB Tony Pollard The Titans opted to retain veteran running back Tony Pollard at the NFL trade deadline after he rushed for 100+ yards in consecutive games (Browns, Bengals) and scored a combined five touchdowns. Pollard didn’t find much rushing success versus the Jaguars, but he did accumulate 66 receiving yards and a touchdown on six catches, including an impressive individual effort on his 32-yard passing score. His steady presence continues to remove the load from Ward’s shoulders.

title: Commanders News: Will Bill play and be a difference-maker vs Bengals?
summary: The Daily Slop – 21 November 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links Articles Commanders Roundtable Bengals […]
full_text: LANDOVER, MARYLAND - AUGUST 18: Jacory Croskey-Merritt #32 of the Washington Commanders is tackled by Eric Gregory #94 of the Cincinnati Bengals during the NFL Preseason 2025 game at Northwest Stadium on August 18, 2025 in Landover, Maryland. (Photo by G Fiume/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Daily Slop – 21 November 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links dark mode 😎 pic.twitter.com/UnDyU9i9c6 — Washington Commanders (@Commanders) November 21, 2026 eyes on Monday pic.twitter.com/BjFTj7MEGj — Washington Commanders (@Commanders) November 21, 2026 Articles Commanders Roundtable Bengals vs Commanders: 3 key matchups to watch The Jayden Daniels Factor Number 5 is getting better every week, and last Thursday night at MetLife he proved it in the most important moment of the season so far. The game-winning touchdown drive in the final minutes was vintage Daniels — poised under pressure, decisive, and clutch when Washington needed him most. His PFF overall grade sits ninth among all 33 qualified quarterbacks in the league, and per PFF, the Daniels-to-Antonio Williams connection carries the second-highest passer rating pairing in the NFL. That’s not a coincidence; it’s a reflection of the route-running and timing chemistry those two have built week over week. The case to force him more targets Monday night is real. Against a Bengals defense that is at its best when it can tee off on a one-dimensional offense, David Blough needs to open the full playbook. That means rolling Daniels out, letting him threaten the edge, exploiting his clean-pocket advantage — PFF ranks him second among all quarterbacks when given a clean pocket — and creating the kind of open-space plays that make the Bengals’ pass rush irrelevant. Monday Night Football on a national stage with playoff hopes on the line. This is the kind of game Jayden Daniels has been building toward all season. Blough needs to trust him, give him room to operate, and let 5 be 5. The talent is there. The moment is here. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Hogs Haven The surprising key to victory over the Bengals Where does WAS have a competitive advantage? Believe it or not, the rushing attack. The Bengals are a poor rushing team, averaging 85 yards per game (30th), while Washington averages 117 (13th). And, for all the gnashing of teeth about the state of the offensive line and the running back stable, Washington is in the top 3rd of the league in rushing yards per attempt (4.3, tied for 11th with the Colts and Jonathan Taylor), while the Bengals are 23rd with 3.9 yards/attempt. Moreover, as I showed in the previous post, rushing defense is the key weakness of the Bengals: they currently rank 20th in rush yards against but 11th on passing yards against. Why play into their hands by getting into a passing showdown when the rushing attack is there for the taking? Remember that Washington abandoned its zone-heavy rushing attack last week in favor of duo (double team blocking on the IOL) and gap, the approaches used in the prior two years. That kind of attack recognizes the limitation of Paul at LG and their Centers as zone players and takes advantage of what they do best. (The other three linemen are zone versatile.) Well, guess what? Rachaad White is a star in duo and gap. In zone, which Washington has emphasized most of the year, White’s average yards per attempt is 3.93 and his success rate is 35% – far below average numbers in the NFL. But when he plays duo, he averages an elite 5.27 YPA and has a success rate of 55%. And when he plays gap, his YPA is an excellent 4.77 and his success rate is 54%. (Data in this paragraph are from Sumer Sports.). It looks like deemphasizing zone and focusing on duo and gap blocking not only fits the OL better, those schemes far better fit their leading rusher. If I’m the OC, I plan on running White at least 18-20 times, almost all in gap and duo. That could give him alone over 100 yards rushing. Doing so will make the play action game work far more effectively, will protect Daniels, will keep the game close, and will set up the kind of passes that can win a close game. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Commanders WR Stefon Diggs on being confident the offense can keep up with the Bengals' offense pic.twitter.com/TfIcPmn8A7 — Martenzie Johnson (@10zJohnson) November 20, 2026 Washington Post (paywall) Cincinnati is contending again after recent struggles; can Jayden Daniels & Washington do the same? The Cincinnati Bengals nearly pulled it off. After the 2021 season, they made an improbable run to the Super Bowl before ultimately falling four points shy of upsetting the Los Angeles Rams. It was only quarterback Joe Burrow’s sophomore NFL season, which fed plenty of optimism about what they could accomplish before his big second contract hit the books. That hope wasn’t shaken when they fell to the eventual Super Bowl champion Kansas City Chiefs in the playoffs a year later. Cincinnati was viewed as a perennial contender that had plenty of financial flexibility to maximize its window. The Bengals haven’t made the postseason since. The Commanders are rightfully focused on the present, not the big picture. That said, their opponent could provide some valuable long-term lessons. When assessing the Burrow-era Bengals’ winding path back to prominence, a road map emerges for the Jayden Daniels-era Commanders to do the same.
